title: Deuteronomy

stories.title: 📜 Deuteronomy 1
summaryBullets: These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel in the wilderness east of the Jordan — in the Arabah opposite Suph — between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab. (1:1).
It is an eleven-day journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea by way of Mount Seir. (1:2).
In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses proclaimed to the Israelites all that the LORD had commanded him concerning them. (1:3).
This was after he had defeated Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and then at Edrei had defeated Og king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth. (1:4).
On the east side of the Jordan in the land of Moab, Moses began to explain this law, saying: (1:5).
The LORD our God said to us at Horeb: “You have stayed at this mountain long enough. (1:6).

Resume your journey and go to the hill country of the Amorites; go to all the neighboring peoples in the Arabah, in the hill country, in the foothills, in the Negev, and along the seacoast to the land of the Canaanites and to Lebanon, as far as the great River Euphrates. (1:7).
See, I have placed the land before you. Enter and possess the land that the LORD swore He would give to your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to their descendants after them.” (1:8).
At that time I said to you, “I cannot carry the burden for you alone. (1:9).
The LORD your God has multiplied you, so that today you are as numerous as the stars in the sky. (1:10).
May the LORD, the God of your fathers, increase you a thousand times over and bless you as He has promised. (1:11).
But how can I bear your troubles, burdens, and disputes all by myself? (1:12).
Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes, and I will appoint them as your leaders.” (1:13).
And you answered me and said, “What you propose to do is good.” (1:14).

So I took the leaders of your tribes, wise and respected men, and appointed them as leaders over you — as commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, and as officers for your tribes. (1:15).
At that time I charged your judges: “Hear the disputes between your brothers, and judge fairly between a man and his brother or a foreign resident. (1:16).

Show no partiality in judging; hear both small and great alike. Do not be intimidated by anyone, for judgment belongs to God. And bring to me any case too difficult for you, and I will hear it.” (1:17).
And at that time I commanded you all the things you were to do. (1:18).

And just as the LORD our God had commanded us, we set out from Horeb and went toward the hill country of the Amorites, through all the vast and terrifying wilderness you have seen. When we reached Kadesh-barnea, (1:19).
I said: “You have reached the hill country of the Amorites, which the LORD our God is giving us. (1:20).
See, the LORD your God has placed the land before you. Go up and take possession of it as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has told you. Do not be afraid or discouraged.” (1:21).
Then all of you approached me and said, “Let us send men ahead of us to search out the land and bring us word of what route to follow and which cities to enter.” (1:22).
The plan seemed good to me, so I selected twelve men from among you, one from each tribe. (1:23).
They left and went up into the hill country, and came to the Valley of Eshcol and spied out the land. (1:24).
They took some of the fruit of the land in their hands, carried it down to us, and brought us word: “It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us.” (1:25).
But you were unwilling to go up; you rebelled against the command of the LORD your God. (1:26).
You grumbled in your tents and said, “Because the LORD hates us, He has brought us out of the land of Egypt to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be annihilated. (1:27).

Where can we go? Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying: ‘The people are larger and taller than we are; the cities are large, with walls up to the heavens. We even saw the descendants of the Anakim there.’” (1:28).
So I said to you: “Do not be terrified or afraid of them! (1:29).
The LORD your God, who goes before you, will fight for you, just as you saw Him do for you in Egypt (1:30).
and in the wilderness, where the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way by which you traveled until you reached this place.” (1:31).
But in spite of all this, you did not trust the LORD your God, (1:32).
who went before you on the journey, in the fire by night and in the cloud by day, to seek out a place for you to camp and to show you the road to travel. (1:33).
When the LORD heard your words, He grew angry and swore an oath, saying, (1:34).
“Not one of the men of this evil generation shall see the good land I swore to give your fathers, (1:35).
except Caleb son of Jephunneh. He will see it, and I will give him and his descendants the land on which he has set foot, because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly.” (1:36).
The LORD was also angry with me on your account, and He said, “Not even you shall enter the land. (1:37).
Joshua son of Nun, who stands before you, will enter it. Encourage him, for he will enable Israel to inherit the land. (1:38).
And the little ones you said would become captives — your children who on that day did not know good from evil — will enter the land that I will give them, and they will possess it. (1:39).
But you are to turn back and head for the wilderness along the route to the Red Sea.” (1:40).

“We have sinned against the LORD,” you replied. “We will go up and fight, as the LORD our God has commanded us.” Then each of you put on his weapons of war, thinking it easy to go up into the hill country. (1:41).
But the LORD said to me, “Tell them not to go up and fight, for I am not with you to keep you from defeat by your enemies.” (1:42).
So I spoke to you, but you would not listen. You rebelled against the command of the LORD and presumptuously went up into the hill country. (1:43).
Then the Amorites who lived in the hills came out against you and chased you like a swarm of bees. They routed you from Seir all the way to Hormah. (1:44).
And you returned and wept before the LORD, but He would not listen to your voice or give ear to you. (1:45).
For this reason you stayed in Kadesh for a long time — a very long time. (1:46).
crossRefs: Numbers 13:1-33: Twelve men are sent to scout Canaan, and ten of them bring back a report that breaks the people's nerve.
Numbers 14:20-25: The LORD swears that none of that generation will see the land, except Caleb who followed Him wholeheartedly.
Exodus 18:21-26: Jethro tells Moses to appoint capable men as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
Numbers 14:39-45: Israel attacks anyway, without the ark or Moses, and is beaten back to Hormah.
Joshua 14:6-14: Caleb, at eighty-five, claims the hill country he was promised for following the LORD wholeheartedly.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים (elleh haddevarim)
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy is laid out like a treaty between a great king and a subject king, the standard legal instrument of that world: a preamble naming the sovereign (1:1-5), a history of what he has already done for the subject (1:6-3:29), the terms (chapters 4 to 26), witnesses with blessings and curses (27 to 28), and instructions to deposit the document and read it aloud on a fixed schedule (31:9-13, 31:24-26). George E. Mendenhall set out the comparison in 1954 and Meredith G. Kline applied it to Deuteronomy in 1963. The form explains why the book runs in this order.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַחַד עָשָׂר יוֹם (achad asar yom)
translationNotes.note: A measured travel figure of the kind a caravan would quote, and the only one Scripture gives for this route. Verse 3 then dates the speech to the fortieth year, and 2:14 puts thirty-eight of those years between Kadesh-barnea and the Brook of Zered. The book opens by laying an eleven-day walk beside a forty-year detour.

translationNotes.term: Commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׂרֵי אֲלָפִים (sarei alafim)
translationNotes.note: A decimal chain of command, the ordinary military structure of the period, put to civil use here as a court system with appeal upward. Jethro proposed it in Exodus 18:21-26. The Hebrew eleph does duty for both 'thousand' and a clan or muster unit, as when Gideon calls his clan the weakest in Manasseh (Judges 6:15), so the groupings may be smaller than the round numbers sound.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא־תַכִּירוּ פָנִים (lo takkiru fanim, 'do not recognize faces')
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew idiom is literally 'do not recognize faces' in court: a judge must not let it matter whose face is standing in front of him. The same idiom stands behind the older English phrase 'respecter of persons'. Deuteronomy 16:19 repeats the rule and gives the reason: a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית (berit), covenant
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy is laid out like a treaty between a great king and a lesser king who serves him, the standard legal instrument of the second millennium BC. George E. Mendenhall set out the parallel in 1954 and Meredith G. Kline developed it in 1963. The parts line up in order: who is speaking (1:1-5), what the great king has already done for the lesser (1:6-4:49), the terms (chapters 5-26), the blessings and curses attached (chapters 27-28), the deposit of the document and its public reading every seven years (31:9-13, 31:26), and the witnesses called (30:19).

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses recalls how God commanded Israel to enter Canaan from Horeb, appointed judges to help lead the people, and describes their rebellion at Kadesh Barnea - their refusal to take the land despite spies' good report, God's anger that barred that generation from entering except Caleb and Joshua, and their failed attempt to fight the Amorites without God's support.

stories.title: 📜 Deuteronomy 2
summaryBullets: Then we turned back and headed for the wilderness by way of the Red Sea, as the LORD had instructed me, and for many days we wandered around Mount Seir. (2:1).
At this time the LORD said to me, (2:2).
“You have been wandering around this hill country long enough; turn to the north (2:3).
and command the people: ‘You will pass through the territory of your brothers, the descendants of Esau, who live in Seir. They will be afraid of you, so you must be very careful. (2:4).
Do not provoke them, for I will not give you any of their land, not even a footprint, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession. (2:5).
You are to pay them in silver for the food you eat and the water you drink.’” (2:6).

Indeed, the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He has watched over your journey through this vast wilderness. The LORD your God has been with you these forty years, and you have lacked nothing. (2:7).

So we passed by our brothers, the descendants of Esau, who live in Seir. We turned away from the Arabah road, which comes up from Elath and Ezion-geber, and traveled along the road of the Wilderness of Moab. (2:8).
Then the LORD said to me, “Do not harass the Moabites or provoke them to war, for I will not give you any of their land, because I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession.” (2:9).
(The Emites used to live there, a people great and many, as tall as the Anakites. (2:10).
Like the Anakites, they were also regarded as Rephaim, though the Moabites called them Emites. (2:11).

The Horites used to live in Seir, but the descendants of Esau drove them out. They destroyed the Horites from before them and settled in their place, just as Israel did in the land that the LORD gave them as their possession.) (2:12).
“Now arise and cross over the Brook of Zered.” So we crossed over the Brook of Zered. (2:13).

The time we spent traveling from Kadesh-barnea until we crossed over the Brook of Zered was thirty-eight years, until that entire generation of fighting men had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them. (2:14).
Indeed, the LORD’s hand was against them, to eliminate them from the camp, until they had all perished. (2:15).
Now when all the fighting men among the people had died, (2:16).
the LORD said to me, (2:17).
“Today you are going to cross the border of Moab at Ar. (2:18).

But when you get close to the Ammonites, do not harass them or provoke them, for I will not give you any of the land of the Ammonites. I have given it to the descendants of Lot as their possession.” (2:19).
(That too was regarded as the land of the Rephaim, who used to live there, though the Ammonites called them Zamzummites. (2:20).
They were a people great and many, as tall as the Anakites. But the LORD destroyed them from before the Ammonites, who drove them out and settled in their place, (2:21).
just as He had done for the descendants of Esau who lived in Seir, when He destroyed the Horites from before them. They drove them out and have lived in their place to this day. (2:22).
And the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, were destroyed by the Caphtorites, who came out of Caphtor and settled in their place.) (2:23).
“Arise, set out, and cross the Arnon Valley. See, I have delivered into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession of it and engage him in battle. (2:24).
This very day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you upon all the nations under heaven. They will hear the reports of you and tremble in anguish because of you.” (2:25).
So from the Wilderness of Kedemoth I sent messengers with an offer of peace to Sihon king of Heshbon, saying, (2:26).
“Let us pass through your land; we will stay on the main road. We will not turn to the right or to the left. (2:27).
You can sell us food to eat and water to drink in exchange for silver. Only let us pass through on foot, (2:28).
just as the descendants of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for us, until we cross the Jordan into the land that the LORD our God is giving us.” (2:29).

But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass through, for the LORD your God had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate, that He might deliver him into your hand, as is the case this day. (2:30).
Then the LORD said to me, “See, I have begun to deliver Sihon and his land over to you. Now begin to conquer and possess his land.” (2:31).
So Sihon and his whole army came out for battle against us at Jahaz. (2:32).
And the LORD our God delivered him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and his whole army. (2:33).
At that time we captured all his cities and devoted to destruction the people of every city, including women and children. We left no survivors. (2:34).
We carried off for ourselves only the livestock and the plunder from the cities we captured. (2:35).
From Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along with the city in the valley, even as far as Gilead, not one city had walls too high for us. The LORD our God gave us all of them. (2:36).
But you did not go near the land of the Ammonites, or the land along the banks of the Jabbok River, or the cities of the hill country, or any place that the LORD our God had forbidden. (2:37).
crossRefs: Numbers 20:14-21: Edom refuses Israel passage along the King's Highway and comes out with an army, so Israel turns aside.
Numbers 21:21-31: Sihon refuses passage, comes out to fight at Jahaz, and loses Heshbon and his whole territory.
Genesis 19:36-38: Moab and Ammon, whose land Israel is forbidden to touch, descend from Lot.
Genesis 36:8-9: Esau settled in the hill country of Seir, the land God had given him as a possession.
Amos 9:7: The LORD brought the Philistines from Caphtor, the migration mentioned in 2:23.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְפָאִים (Rephaim) - אֵמִים (Emim) - זַמְזֻמִּים (Zamzummim)
translationNotes.note: Verses 10 to 23 are a set of asides explaining who lived in these lands before the present owners, and they give the local names for the same tall people: Moab called them Emites, Ammon called them Zamzummites, and both were reckoned Rephaim, like the Anakim. The last aside notes that the Caphtorites displaced the Avvim near Gaza. Caphtor is the homeland the prophets name for the Philistines (Amos 9:7).

translationNotes.term: The Brook of Zered and the Arnon Valley
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחַל זֶרֶד (nachal Zered) - נַחַל אַרְנוֹן (nachal Arnon)
translationNotes.note: Nachal means a seasonal streambed, not a brook you step over. These two cut the Transjordan plateau into blocks and served as national borders because crossing them is hard. The Arnon, the modern Wadi Mujib, runs in a gorge on the order of 3,000 feet from the plateau rim down to the water. Crossing the Zered marks the end of the wandering (2:14) and crossing the Arnon opens the campaign (2:24).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֶּסֶף (kesef, 'silver')
translationNotes.note: The same Hebrew word means both silver and money, because payment was weighed metal rather than coin. The instruction in 2:6 and the offer to Sihon in 2:28 are the ordinary terms for a large body of people crossing another nation's territory: buy your food and water, stay on the road, take nothing. Israel is told to move through Edom, Moab, and Ammon as a paying customer, not an army.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁלֹשִׁים וּשְׁמֹנֶה שָׁנָה (sheloshim u-shemoneh shanah)
translationNotes.note: The count in 2:14 runs from Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Zered, not from Egypt. Add the roughly two years from the exodus to the failure at Kadesh and the total comes to the forty years of the sentence in Numbers 14:33-34. The chapter is showing that the arithmetic of the oath was kept exactly.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel journeys around Edom and Moab without conflict, as God forbids provocation against these lands reserved for others; after thirty-eight years of wandering eliminate the old generation, Israel defeats Sihon the Amorite king and conquers all his towns while respecting the boundaries God set for Ammonite territory.

stories.title: 📜 Deuteronomy 3
summaryBullets: Then we turned and went up the road to Bashan, and Og king of Bashan and his whole army came out to meet us in battle at Edrei. (3:1).

But the LORD said to me, “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land. Do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon.” (3:2).
So the LORD our God also delivered Og king of Bashan and his whole army into our hands. We struck them down until no survivor was left. (3:3).
At that time we captured all sixty of his cities. There was not a single city we failed to take — the entire region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan. (3:4).
All these cities were fortified with high walls and gates and bars, and there were many more unwalled villages. (3:5).
We devoted them to destruction, as we had done to Sihon king of Heshbon, utterly destroying the men, women, and children of every city. (3:6).
But all the livestock and plunder of the cities we carried off for ourselves. (3:7).
At that time we took from the two kings of the Amorites the land across the Jordan, from the Arnon Valley as far as Mount Hermon — (3:8).
which the Sidonians call Sirion but the Amorites call Senir — (3:9).
all the cities of the plateau, all of Gilead, and all of Bashan as far as the cities of Salecah and Edrei in the kingdom of Og. (3:10).
(For only Og king of Bashan had remained of the remnant of the Rephaim. His bed of iron, nine cubits long and four cubits wide, is still in Rabbah of the Ammonites.) (3:11).
So at that time we took possession of this land. To the Reubenites and Gadites I gave the land beyond Aroer along the Arnon Valley, and half the hill country of Gilead, along with its cities. (3:12).

To the half-tribe of Manasseh I gave the rest of Gilead and all of Bashan, the kingdom of Og. (The entire region of Argob, the whole territory of Bashan, used to be called the land of the Rephaim.) (3:13).

Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, took the whole region of Argob as far as the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites. He renamed Bashan after himself, Havvoth-jair, by which it is called to this day. (3:14).
To Machir I gave Gilead, (3:15).
and to the Reubenites and Gadites I gave the territory from Gilead to the Arnon Valley (the middle of the valley was the border) and up to the Jabbok River, the border of the Ammonites. (3:16).
The Jordan River in the Arabah bordered it from Chinnereth to the Sea of the Arabah (the Salt Sea) with the slopes of Pisgah to the east. (3:17).
At that time I commanded you: “The LORD your God has given you this land to possess. All your men of valor are to cross over, armed for battle, ahead of your brothers, the Israelites. (3:18).
But your wives, your children, and your livestock— I know that you have much livestock— may remain in the cities I have given you, (3:19).

until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as He has to you, and they too have taken possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them across the Jordan. Then each of you may return to the possession I have given you.” (3:20).
And at that time I commanded Joshua: “Your own eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. The LORD will do the same to all the kingdoms you are about to enter. (3:21).
Do not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God Himself will fight for you.” (3:22).
At that time I also pleaded with the LORD: (3:23).
“O Lord GOD, You have begun to show Your greatness and power to Your servant. For what god in heaven or on earth can perform such works and mighty acts as Yours? (3:24).
Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan — that pleasant hill country as well as Lebanon!” (3:25).
But the LORD was angry with me on account of you, and He would not listen to me. “That is enough,” the LORD said to me. “Do not speak to Me again about this matter. (3:26).
Go to the top of Pisgah and look to the west and north and south and east. See the land with your own eyes, for you will not cross this Jordan. (3:27).
But commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him, for he will cross over ahead of the people and enable them to inherit the land that you will see.” (3:28).
So we stayed in the valley opposite Beth-peor. (3:29).
crossRefs: Numbers 21:33-35: Og king of Bashan comes out at Edrei, and Israel strikes him down and takes his land.
Numbers 32:28-33: Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh are given the eastern land on condition that they cross over armed and fight first.
Numbers 20:9-12: Moses strikes the rock at Meribah, and God tells him he will not bring the assembly into the land.
Joshua 1:12-15: Joshua holds the eastern tribes to the promise made here, that their fighting men cross ahead of their brothers.
Deuteronomy 34:1-4: Moses climbs Pisgah at last and is shown the whole land he is told he will not enter.

translationNotes.term: His bed of iron, nine cubits long and four cubits wide
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶרֶשׂ בַּרְזֶל (eres barzel)
translationNotes.note: At roughly 18 inches to the cubit that is about 13 feet 6 inches by 6 feet. The Hebrew eres is a couch or bedstead and can also mean a bier or a sarcophagus, which is how many read it here. The verse says the object was still on show at Rabbah, the Ammonite capital on the site of modern Amman, which is why the writer can cite it: readers could go and look.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶרְמוֹן (Hermon) - שִׂרְיֹן (Siryon) - שְׂנִיר (Senir)
translationNotes.note: One mountain under three national names, given because each neighbor called it something different. Hermon rises to about 9,230 feet, the highest ground in the region and the only summit that holds snow through the summer; its melt feeds the headwaters of the Jordan. It marks the far northern limit of the conquest described here.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּנֶּרֶת (Kinneret)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament name for the lake the Gospels call the Sea of Galilee. It is built on the same consonants as kinnor, the Hebrew harp or lyre, and the lake has that outline. Verse 17 uses it as a survey marker, running the border down the Jordan from Chinnereth to the Salt Sea, which is the Dead Sea.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פִּסְגָּה (Pisgah)
translationNotes.note: Not a single peak but a ridge or headland in the Abarim range on the Moabite plateau, east of the Dead Sea. Mount Nebo is one of its heads (Deuteronomy 34:1). From that rim the ground drops more than 4,000 feet to the Jordan valley, which is why Moses is told to look west, north, south, and east and see the land with his own eyes.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel defeats Og king of Bashan and takes all sixty of his fortified cities; Moses then distributes the conquered eastern territory to the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh, while the LORD denies his request to cross the Jordan and commands him to prepare Joshua as his successor.

headings.text: Land Division East of the Jordan
Moses Forbidden to Cross the Jordan

stories.title: 📜 Deuteronomy 4
summaryBullets: Hear now, O Israel, the statutes and ordinances I am teaching you to follow, so that you may live and may enter and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, is giving you. (4:1).
You must not add to or subtract from what I command you, so that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I am giving you. (4:2).
Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor, for the LORD your God destroyed from among you all who followed Baal of Peor. (4:3).
But you who held fast to the LORD your God are alive to this day, every one of you. (4:4).
See, I have taught you statutes and ordinances just as the LORD my God has commanded me, so that you may follow them in the land that you are about to enter and possess. (4:5).

Observe them carefully, for this will show your wisdom and understanding in the sight of the peoples, who will hear of all these statutes and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” (4:6).
For what nation is great enough to have a god as near to them as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call on Him? (4:7).
And what nation is great enough to have righteous statutes and ordinances like this entire law I set before you today? (4:8).

Only be on your guard and diligently watch yourselves, so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen, and so that they do not slip from your heart as long as you live. Teach them to your children and grandchildren. (4:9).

The day you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, the LORD said to me, “Gather the people before Me to hear My words, so that they may learn to fear Me all the days they live on the earth, and that they may teach them to their children.” (4:10).
You came near and stood at the base of the mountain, a mountain blazing with fire to the heavens, with black clouds and deep darkness. (4:11).
And the LORD spoke to you out of the fire. You heard the sound of the words but saw no form; there was only a voice. (4:12).
He declared to you His covenant, which He commanded you to follow — the Ten Commandments that He wrote on two tablets of stone. (4:13).
At that time the LORD commanded me to teach you the statutes and ordinances you are to follow in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess. (4:14).
So since you saw no form of any kind on the day the LORD spoke to you out of the fire at Horeb, be careful (4:15).
that you do not act corruptly and make an idol for yourselves of any form or shape, whether in the likeness of a male or female, (4:16).
of any beast that is on the earth or bird that flies in the air, (4:17).
or of any creature that crawls on the ground or fish that is in the waters below. (4:18).

When you look to the heavens and see the sun and moon and stars— all the host of heaven— do not be enticed to bow down and worship what the LORD your God has apportioned to all the nations under heaven. (4:19).
Yet the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be the people of His inheritance, as you are today. (4:20).
The LORD, however, was angry with me on account of you, and He swore that I would not cross the Jordan to enter the good land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance. (4:21).
For I will not be crossing the Jordan, because I must die in this land. But you shall cross over and take possession of that good land. (4:22).
Be careful that you do not forget the covenant of the LORD your God that He made with you; do not make an idol for yourselves in the form of anything He has forbidden you. (4:23).
For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God. (4:24).

After you have children and grandchildren and you have been in the land a long time, if you then act corruptly and make an idol of any form— doing evil in the sight of the LORD your God and provoking Him to anger— (4:25).

I call heaven and earth as witnesses against you this day that you will quickly perish from the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess. You will not live long upon it, but will be utterly destroyed. (4:26).
Then the LORD will scatter you among the peoples, and only a few of you will survive among the nations to which the LORD will drive you. (4:27).
And there you will serve man-made gods of wood and stone, which cannot see or hear or eat or smell. (4:28).
But if from there you will seek the LORD your God, you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul. (4:29).
When you are in distress and all these things have happened to you, then in later days you will return to the LORD your God and listen to His voice. (4:30).
For the LORD your God is a merciful God; He will not abandon you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers, which He swore to them by oath. (4:31).

Indeed, ask now from one end of the heavens to the other about the days that long preceded you, from the day that God created man on earth: Has anything as great as this ever happened or been reported? (4:32).
Has a people ever heard the voice of God speaking out of the fire, as you have, and lived? (4:33).

Or has any god tried to take as his own a nation out of another nation — by trials, signs, wonders, and war, by a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and by great terrors — as the LORD your God did for you in Egypt, before your eyes? (4:34).
You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him. (4:35).
He let you hear His voice from heaven to discipline you, and on earth He showed you His great fire, and you heard His words out of the fire. (4:36).
Because He loved your fathers, He chose their descendants after them and brought you out of Egypt by His presence and great power, (4:37).
to drive out before you nations greater and mightier than you, and to bring you into their land and give it to you for your inheritance, as it is this day. (4:38).
Know therefore this day and take to heart that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below; there is no other. (4:39).

Keep His statutes and commandments, which I am giving you today, so that you and your children after you may prosper, and that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time. (4:40).
Then Moses set aside three cities across the Jordan to the east (4:41).
to which a manslayer could flee after killing his neighbor unintentionally without prior malice. To save one’s own life, he could flee to one of these cities: (4:42).
Bezer in the wilderness on the plateau belonging to the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead belonging to the Gadites, or Golan in Bashan belonging to the Manassites. (4:43).
This is the law that Moses set before the Israelites. (4:44).
These are the testimonies, statutes, and ordinances that Moses proclaimed to them after they had come out of Egypt, (4:45).

while they were in the valley across the Jordan facing Beth-peor in the land of Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon and was defeated by Moses and the Israelites after they had come out of Egypt. (4:46).
They took possession of the land belonging to Sihon and to Og king of Bashan — the two Amorite kings across the Jordan to the east — (4:47).
extending from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley as far as Mount Siyon (that is, Hermon), (4:48).
including all the Arabah on the east side of the Jordan and as far as the Sea of the Arabah, below the slopes of Pisgah. (4:49).
crossRefs: Exodus 20:1-21: The day at Horeb when the mountain burned, the people heard the voice out of the fire, and stood far off.
Numbers 25:1-9: What happened at Baal-peor, which Moses says their own eyes saw.
Numbers 35:9-15: Six cities of refuge are commanded, three east of the Jordan and three in Canaan.
Joshua 20:7-8: The six cities are named and set apart, including Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan.
Jeremiah 29:13-14: You will seek Me and find Me when you search with all your heart, and I will gather you from every place I banished you.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּעַל פְּעוֹר (Baʿal Peʿor), Greek: Βεελφεγώρ (Beelphegōr), Aramaic: בעל פעור (Baʿal Peʿor)
translationNotes.note: A Moabite idol worshiped with sexual immorality; many Israelites perished for joining in (Numbers 25).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִקְלָט (miqlat), Greek: φυγή (phygē), Aramaic: מקלטא (miqlata)
translationNotes.note: Safe place for those who killed unintentionally until trial.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוּר הַבַּרְזֶל (kur habbarzel)
translationNotes.note: A kur is a smelting furnace, the kind built to drive metal out of ore, not a household fire. The image is of Egypt as a crucible that burned everything else away. The same phrase is used of Egypt by Solomon at the temple dedication (1 Kings 8:51) and by Jeremiah (11:4), so it became a fixed way of naming the bondage.

translationNotes.term: You must not add to or subtract from
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא תֹסִפוּ ... וְלֹא תִגְרְעוּ (lo tosifu ... ve-lo tigreu)
translationNotes.note: A standard protective clause on ancient legal and treaty documents, forbidding either party to alter the text after it is sealed. Deuteronomy uses it twice, here and at 12:32, and the same formula closes the Bible at Revelation 22:18-19. It is a clause about the document, not about interpretation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֶּצֶר (Betser), from a root meaning to cut off or make inaccessible
translationNotes.note: Bezer is not a stray name. It is a town on the mishor, the flat tableland east of the Jordan in Reuben's territory, and Moses sets it apart here as the first of three cities of refuge on that side of the river (4:41-43). Joshua 20:8 lists it again with the same description, and Joshua 21:36 makes it a Levite town. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite victory inscription of the ninth century BC found at Dhiban in Jordan in 1868, has its king say in line 27 that he built Bezer because it lay in ruins.

translationNotes.term: the three cities across the Jordan
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָרֵי מִקְלָט (arei miqlat), cities of intake or asylum
translationNotes.note: Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan are set out north to south across the eastern territory so that no one living there was far from one (4:43). A man who killed by accident had to reach a gate before the dead man's family reached him. Three more were later named west of the Jordan, at Joshua 20:7, making six in all, and Deuteronomy 19:3 orders roads built and the land divided in three so the distance stays short.

translationNotes.term: Sihon and Og, Heshbon and Bashan
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶשְׁבּוֹן (Cheshbon) - בָּשָׁן (Bashan)
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 4:46-47 fixes where Moses is standing by naming the two Amorite kings Israel had just beaten. Sihon ruled from Heshbon on the plateau east of the Dead Sea; Og ruled Bashan, the high grassland northeast of the Sea of Galilee, famous for its cattle and oaks, which is why Amos 4:1 calls the rich women of Samaria cows of Bashan and Psalm 22:12 speaks of strong bulls of Bashan. The territory described runs from the Arnon gorge in the south to Mount Hermon in the north.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses charges Israel to keep the statutes without adding or subtracting, recalling that at Horeb they heard the LORD’s voice from the fire but saw no form, so they must not make an idol of any shape or worship the host of heaven. He warns that idolatry will scatter them among the nations, where they will find the LORD if they seek him with all their heart, for the LORD is God and there is no other; he then sets apart Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan as cities of refuge east of the Jordan.

stories.title: 📖 Deuteronomy 5
summaryBullets: Then Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: Hear, O Israel, the statutes and ordinances that I declare in your hearing this day. Learn them and observe them carefully. (5:1).
The LORD our God made a covenant with us at Horeb. (5:2).
He did not make this covenant with our fathers, but with all of us who are alive here today. (5:3).
The LORD spoke with you face to face out of the fire on the mountain. (5:4).
At that time I was standing between the LORD and you to declare to you the word of the LORD, because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain. And He said: (5:5).
“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (5:6).
You shall have no other gods before Me. (5:7).
You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath. (5:8).

You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me, (5:9).
but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments. (5:10).
You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain. (5:11).
Observe the Sabbath day by keeping it holy, as the LORD your God has commanded you. (5:12).
Six days you shall labor and do all your work, (5:13).

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work— neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant, nor your ox or donkey or any of your livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates, so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do. (5:14).

Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the Sabbath day. (5:15).
Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God has commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. (5:16).
You shall not murder. (5:17).
You shall not commit adultery. (5:18).
You shall not steal. (5:19).
You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. (5:20).

You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. You shall not covet your neighbor’s house or field, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.” (5:21).

The LORD spoke these commandments in a loud voice to your whole assembly out of the fire, the cloud, and the deep darkness on the mountain; He added nothing more. And He wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me. (5:22).
And when you heard the voice out of the darkness while the mountain was blazing with fire, all the heads of your tribes and your elders approached me, (5:23).
and you said, “Behold, the LORD our God has shown us His glory and greatness, and we have heard His voice out of the fire. Today we have seen that a man can live even if God speaks with him. (5:24).
But now, why should we die? For this great fire will consume us, and we will die, if we hear the voice of the LORD our God any longer. (5:25).
For who of all flesh has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the fire, as we have, and survived? (5:26).
Go near and listen to all that the LORD our God says. Then you can tell us everything the LORD our God tells you; we will listen and obey.” (5:27).
And the LORD heard the words you spoke to me, and He said to me, “I have heard the words that these people have spoken to you. They have done well in all that they have spoken. (5:28).
If only they had such a heart to fear Me and keep all My commandments always, so that it might be well with them and with their children forever. (5:29).
Go and tell them: ‘Return to your tents.’ (5:30).
But you stand here with Me, that I may speak to you all the commandments and statutes and ordinances you are to teach them to follow in the land that I am giving them to possess.” (5:31).
So be careful to do as the LORD your God has commanded you; you are not to turn aside to the right or to the left. (5:32).
You must walk in all the ways that the LORD your God has commanded you, so that you may live and prosper and prolong your days in the land that you will possess. (5:33).
crossRefs: Exodus 20:1-17: The Ten Commandments as first spoken at Sinai.
Exodus 20:18-21: The people stand at a distance in terror and ask Moses to hear God for them.
Exodus 20:11: The sabbath command in Exodus is grounded in the six days of creation; here in 5:15 it is grounded in the exodus from slavery.
Exodus 34:27-28: Moses writes the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments, on the tablets.
Deuteronomy 18:15-18: The people's request that Moses speak for them becomes the ground for the promise of a prophet like him.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁמַע (shemaʿ), Greek: ἄκουε (akoue), Aramaic: שמע (shema)
translationNotes.note: Means 'hear' or 'listen with intent to obey'; refers to Deuteronomy 6:4-5.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲשֵׁרִים (ʾasherim), Greek: ἄλσος (alsos), Aramaic: אשריא (ashreya)
translationNotes.note: Wooden poles or groves representing the goddess Asherah, often set up beside altars.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא תִּרְצָח (lōʾ tirtsaḥ), Greek (LXX): οὐ φονεύσεις (ou phoneuseis), Aramaic: לָא תִּקְטוּל (lā tiqtul)
translationNotes.note: The command forbids murder (unlawful, intentional killing). It does not ban every kind of killing (e.g., just war, self-defense, or court-ordered execution).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טוֹטָפֹת (ṭotafot), Greek: φυλακτήρια (phylaktēria), Aramaic: טוטפתא (ṭoṭafta)
translationNotes.note: Later worn as phylacteries; here, figurative for constant remembrance of God’s commands.

About two thirds of a mile (1 km); the rabbinic limit on travel from one's dwelling on the Sabbath, derived from the camp boundaries in Exodus 16:29 and Numbers 35:5. Acts 1:12 places the Mount of Olives this distance from Jerusalem.
translationNotes.original: Greek: σαββάτου ἔχον ὁδόν (sabbatou echon hodon)

translationNotes.note: The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁבָּת (shabbat); Greek: σάββατον (sabbaton)

translationNotes.term: Manslayer and murderer are one word
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹצֵחַ (rotseach), one who kills - בִּשְׁגָגָה (bishgagah), unintentionally
translationNotes.note: The command at 5:17 uses the verb ratsach, and the noun from that root covers both the murderer and the man who kills by accident. Numbers 35:11 applies rotseach to the man who strikes someone down bishgagah, unintentionally, and sends him to a city of refuge, and 35:25 uses the same noun for the man the congregation rescues from the avenger. One Hebrew word spans the whole range, the way English 'homicide' does, and the tests that separate the two cases are set out at Numbers 35:16-23 and Deuteronomy 19:4-13.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְזָכַרְתָּ כִּי־עֶבֶד הָיִיתָ (vezakharta ki eved hayita), 'and you shall remember that you were a slave'
translationNotes.note: Exodus 20:11 grounds the sabbath command in creation, because the LORD rested on the seventh day. Deuteronomy 5:15 grounds the same command in the exodus, because you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD brought you out. The two chapters give the same commandment with different reasons attached, and 5:14 spells out who the rest covers: son, daughter, male and female servant, ox, donkey, livestock, and the foreigner inside your gates.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְלֹא יָסָף (velo yasaf), 'and He added no more' - עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדְּבָרִים (aseret hadevarim), 'the ten words'
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 5:22 says the LORD spoke these words to the whole assembly out of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, with a great voice, and added no more. Everything else in the law comes through Moses, and 5:23-31 explains why: the people asked him to go and listen for them because they were afraid they would die. The ten came direct and public; the rest came mediated.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses recites the Ten Commandments that God spoke at Horeb, instructing Israel to learn and follow them; the people, terrified by God's voice from the fire, ask Moses to receive God's further instructions on their behalf.

stories.title: 📖 Deuteronomy 6
summaryBullets: These are the commandments and statutes and ordinances that the LORD your God has instructed me to teach you to follow in the land that you are about to enter and possess, (6:1).

so that you and your children and grandchildren may fear the LORD your God all the days of your lives by keeping all His statutes and commandments that I give you, and so that your days may be prolonged. (6:2).
Hear, O Israel, and be careful to observe them, so that you may prosper and multiply greatly in a land flowing with milk and honey, just as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you. (6:3).
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. (6:4).
And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. (6:5).
These words I am commanding you today are to be upon your hearts. (6:6).
And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. (6:7).
Tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. (6:8).
Write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates. (6:9).

And when the LORD your God brings you into the land He swore to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, that He would give you— a land with great and splendid cities that you did not build, (6:10).

with houses full of every good thing with which you did not fill them, with wells that you did not dig, and with vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant— and when you eat and are satisfied, (6:11).
be careful not to forget the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (6:12).
Fear the LORD your God, serve Him only, and take your oaths in His name. (6:13).
Do not follow other gods, the gods of the peoples around you. (6:14).
For the LORD your God, who is among you, is a jealous God. Otherwise the anger of the LORD your God will be kindled against you, and He will wipe you off the face of the earth. (6:15).
Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah. (6:16).
You are to diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God and the testimonies and statutes He has given you. (6:17).
Do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD, so that it may be well with you and that you may enter and possess the good land that the LORD your God swore to give your fathers, (6:18).
driving out all your enemies before you, as the LORD has said. (6:19).
In the future, when your son asks, “What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the LORD our God has commanded you?” (6:20).
then you are to tell him, “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand. (6:21).
Before our eyes the LORD inflicted great and devastating signs and wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh, and on all his household. (6:22).
But He brought us out from there to lead us in and give us the land that He had sworn to our fathers. (6:23).
And the LORD commanded us to observe all these statutes and to fear the LORD our God, that we may always be prosperous and preserved, as we are to this day. (6:24).
And if we are careful to observe every one of these commandments before the LORD our God, as He has commanded us, then that will be our righteousness.” (6:25).
crossRefs: Mark 12:29-30: Jesus quotes the Shema as the first of all the commandments.
Exodus 17:1-7: What happened at Massah, where Israel quarreled over water and tested the LORD.
Matthew 4:7: Jesus answers the tempter with 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test', quoting 6:16.
Deuteronomy 11:18-21: The same charge repeated: fix these words on your hand, your forehead, your doorposts, and your gates.
Matthew 23:5: Men widen their phylacteries to be seen, the boxes worn in obedience to this command.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד (Shema Yisrael, YHWH Eloheinu, YHWH echad)
translationNotes.note: The sentence at 6:4 is named after its first word, shema, hear. Hebrew shema carries obedience with it, not just sound; the same verb is what a servant does when he listens to an order. Verse 6:5 attaches the whole command to love God with all your heart, soul and strength, and Jesus names this pair the greatest commandment at Mark 12:29-30, quoting 6:4 and 6:5 together. It has been Israel's daily confession since antiquity, said morning and evening.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טֹטָפֹת (totafot), bands on the forehead - מְזוּזָה (mezuzah), doorpost
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 6:8-9 orders the words bound on the hand and forehead and written on the doorframes, and Israel took it literally as well as figuratively. Small leather capsules about one inch by three quarters of an inch, holding parchment strips, were recovered from the caves at Qumran near the Dead Sea, the oldest surviving examples; the strips carry Exodus 13:1-10 and 13:11-16 with Deuteronomy 6:4-9 and 11:13-21. Greek speakers called the boxes phylakteria, guards or amulets, which is where the English word phylactery comes from. Jesus refers to men widening theirs at Matthew 23:5.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַסָּה (Massah), 'testing'
translationNotes.note: Verse 6:16 forbids testing God as Israel did at Massah, and the reader needs Exodus 17:1-7 to know what happened: no water at Rephidim, the people quarrelled with Moses and asked whether the LORD was among them or not, and the place was named for the question. Jesus quotes this verse word for word at Matthew 4:7 and Luke 4:12, answering the second temptation with it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּתִּים מְלֵאִים כָּל־טוּב (battim meleim kol-tuv), 'houses full of every good thing'
translationNotes.note: Verses 6:10-11 list what Israel is about to inherit without having made any of it: great and good cities they did not build, houses filled with goods they did not fill, wells they did not dig, vineyards and olive groves they did not plant. Olive trees take a decade or more to come into full bearing and cisterns had to be cut out of rock by hand, so the list names the slowest and costliest capital in that world. Verse 6:12 gives the warning attached to it, that having eaten and been satisfied they would forget.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses teaches Israel to love the LORD their God with all their heart, soul, and strength, and to keep his commands by teaching them to their children and binding them as reminders; he warns them not to forget the LORD or follow other gods once they occupy the promised land of prosperity.

stories.title: 📖 Deuteronomy 7
summaryBullets: When the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to possess, and He drives out before you many nations— the Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, seven nations larger and stronger than you— (7:1).
and when the LORD your God has delivered them over to you to defeat them, then you must devote them to complete destruction. Make no treaty with them and show them no mercy. (7:2).
Do not intermarry with them. Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons, (7:3).
because they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD will burn against you, and He will swiftly destroy you. (7:4).
Instead, this is what you are to do to them: tear down their altars, smash their sacred pillars, cut down their Asherah poles, and burn their idols in the fire. (7:5).
For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all peoples on the face of the earth. (7:6).
The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples. (7:7).

But because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers, He brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt. (7:8).
Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments. (7:9).
But those who hate Him He repays to their faces with destruction; He will not hesitate to repay to his face the one who hates Him. (7:10).
So keep the commandments and statutes and ordinances that I am giving you to follow this day. (7:11).
If you listen to these ordinances and keep them carefully, then the LORD your God will keep His covenant and the loving devotion that He swore to your fathers. (7:12).

He will love you and bless you and multiply you. He will bless the fruit of your womb and the produce of your land— your grain, new wine, and oil, the young of your herds and the lambs of your flocks— in the land that He swore to your fathers to give you. (7:13).
You will be blessed above all peoples; among you there will be no barren man or woman or livestock. (7:14).
And the LORD will remove from you all sickness. He will not lay upon you any of the terrible diseases you knew in Egypt, but He will inflict them on all who hate you. (7:15).
You must destroy all the peoples the LORD your God will deliver to you. Do not look on them with pity. Do not worship their gods, for that will be a snare to you. (7:16).
You may say in your heart, “These nations are greater than we are; how can we drive them out?” (7:17).
But do not be afraid of them. Be sure to remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and all Egypt: (7:18).

the great trials that you saw, the signs and wonders, and the mighty hand and outstretched arm by which the LORD your God brought you out. The LORD your God will do the same to all the peoples you now fear. (7:19).
Moreover, the LORD your God will send the hornet against them until even the survivors hiding from you have perished. (7:20).
Do not be terrified by them, for the LORD your God, who is among you, is a great and awesome God. (7:21).
The LORD your God will drive out these nations before you little by little. You will not be enabled to eliminate them all at once, or the wild animals would multiply around you. (7:22).
But the LORD your God will give them over to you and throw them into great confusion, until they are destroyed. (7:23).
He will hand their kings over to you, and you will wipe out their names from under heaven. No one will be able to stand against you; you will annihilate them. (7:24).

You must burn up the images of their gods; do not covet the silver and gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, or you will be ensnared by it; for it is detestable to the LORD your God. (7:25).

And you must not bring any detestable thing into your house, or you, like it, will be set apart for destruction. You are to utterly detest and abhor it, because it is set apart for destruction. (7:26).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:11-16: The same order to break down altars and refuse marriage alliances with the peoples of the land.
Exodus 23:28-30: God will drive them out little by little, not in a single year, so the land does not go wild.
Joshua 23:11-13: Joshua warns that marrying the survivors will make them a snare, a whip, and thorns in your eyes.
Judges 3:5-7: Israel marries into the nations and serves the Baals, exactly as warned.
1 Kings 11:1-8: Solomon's foreign wives turn his heart after other gods in his old age.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲשֵׁרָה (asherah), plural אֲשֵׁרִים (asherim)
translationNotes.note: Wooden cult objects, planted upright beside a Canaanite altar, named for the goddess Asherah, who is known from the Ugaritic texts recovered at Ras Shamra in Syria from 1929 onward as the consort of the high god El. Because they were set into the ground and made of wood, the standing orders are always to cut them down and burn them, as at 7:5 and 12:3. 2 Kings 23:6 records Josiah taking one out of the temple itself and burning it in the Kidron valley.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁבְעָה גוֹיִם רַבִּים וַעֲצוּמִים (shivah goyim rabbim va-atsumim), 'seven nations greater and stronger'
translationNotes.note: Verse 7:1 names them: Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites. These are the peoples of the land, not a general term for foreigners; the Hittites ran an empire in Anatolia whose royal archive was dug up at Bogazkoy from 1906, and the Jebusites held the ridge that later became Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Verse 7:7 adds the comparison the chapter turns on, that Israel was the fewest of all peoples.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵרֶם (cherem), the verb הַחֲרֵם תַּחֲרִים (hacharem tacharim)
translationNotes.note: Cherem means to put something permanently beyond ordinary use by handing it over to God, and Leviticus 27:28-29 states that what is placed under it can never be redeemed or sold. Verse 7:2 applies it to the seven nations and forbids any treaty with them, and 7:25-26 extends it to their idols and the silver and gold on them, which may not be taken as plunder. The reason given is at 7:4, that intermarriage would turn Israel's sons to other gods.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְעַט מְעָט (meat meat)
translationNotes.note: Verse 7:22 states the pace and the reason: the nations will be driven out gradually, because clearing the land too fast would let the wild animals multiply. That is a practical observation about a farmed landscape, where predators and boar move back in as soon as the fields go untended. Exodus 23:29-30 gives the same rule in the same words, and Judges 1 records how much land was in fact still held when the conquest slowed.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses instructs Israel to totally destroy the seven Canaanite nations without making treaties or intermarrying, destroying their altars and idols, because Israel is God's chosen and treasured people. God promises to drive out these nations gradually and bless Israel abundantly if they obey his commands and avoid their gods.

stories.title: 📖 Deuteronomy 8
summaryBullets: You must carefully follow every commandment I am giving you today, so that you may live and multiply, and enter and possess the land that the LORD swore to give your fathers. (8:1).

Remember that these forty years the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments. (8:2).

He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your fathers had known, so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD. (8:3).
Your clothing did not wear out and your feet did not swell during these forty years. (8:4).
So know in your heart that just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you. (8:5).
Therefore you shall keep the commandments of the LORD your God, walking in His ways and fearing Him. (8:6).
For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks and fountains and springs that flow through the valleys and hills; (8:7).
a land of wheat, barley, vines, fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of olive oil and honey; (8:8).
a land where you will eat food without scarcity, where you will lack nothing; a land whose rocks are iron and whose hills are ready to be mined for copper. (8:9).
When you eat and are satisfied, you are to bless the LORD your God for the good land that He has given you. (8:10).
Be careful not to forget the LORD your God by failing to keep His commandments and ordinances and statutes, which I am giving you this day. (8:11).
Otherwise, when you eat and are satisfied, when you build fine houses in which to dwell, (8:12).
and when your herds and flocks grow large and your silver and gold increase and all that you have is multiplied, (8:13).
then your heart will become proud, and you will forget the LORD your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (8:14).
He led you through the vast and terrifying wilderness with its venomous snakes and scorpions, a thirsty and waterless land. He brought you water from the rock of flint. (8:15).
He fed you in the wilderness with manna that your fathers had not known, in order to humble you and test you, so that in the end He might cause you to prosper. (8:16).
You might say in your heart, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.” (8:17).
But remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth, in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers even to this day. (8:18).
If you ever forget the LORD your God and go after other gods to worship and bow down to them, I testify against you today that you will surely perish. (8:19).
Like the nations that the LORD has destroyed before you, so you will perish if you do not obey the LORD your God. (8:20).
crossRefs: Matthew 4:4: Jesus answers the tempter with 'Man shall not live on bread alone', quoting 8:3.
Exodus 16:13-35: The manna, a food the fathers had never known, given every morning for forty years.
Deuteronomy 8:15: The wilderness with its venomous snakes and scorpions, and water brought out of flint.
Hosea 13:6: When they were fed they were satisfied, their hearts grew proud, and they forgot Me.
Deuteronomy 6:10-12: The same warning: when you eat and are full in houses you did not build, do not forget the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָן (man)
translationNotes.note: The name comes from the question the people asked when they first saw it, man hu, what is it (Exodus 16:15). Exodus 16:31 describes it as white like coriander seed and tasting of wafers made with honey, and Numbers 11:7-8 adds that it was ground in handmills or crushed in mortars, boiled, and made into cakes that tasted of oil. It fell for forty years and stopped the day after Israel first ate the produce of Canaan (Joshua 5:12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַרְבָּעִים שָׁנָה (arbaim shanah)
translationNotes.note: The length was set as a sentence, not a wandering. Numbers 14:33-34 fixes it at one year for each of the forty days the twelve men spent scouting the land, so that the generation that refused to go up would die in the wilderness. That is the span verse 2 is telling them to remember.

translationNotes.term: A land of wheat, barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, oil, and honey
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דְּבַשׁ (devash)
translationNotes.note: These seven crops are the working agriculture of the land, and they set the calendar. Barley ripened first, in spring, and its sheaf was waved before any of the harvest could be eaten (Leviticus 23:10-11); wheat came in weeks later at the Feast of Weeks (Leviticus 23:15-17); grapes, figs, and olives came in late summer and autumn. Devash covers both bee honey and the thick syrup boiled down from dates or grapes.

translationNotes.term: Rocks are iron, hills ready to be mined for copper
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְחֹשֶׁת (nechoshet)
translationNotes.note: This is a specific claim about a specific region. Copper was mined and smelted in the Arabah, the rift valley running south from the Dead Sea toward the Gulf of Aqaba, where ancient shafts, galleries, and slag heaps survive at Timna on the western side and at Feinan on the eastern side. Feinan is Punon, one of the camps listed on Israel's own wilderness route in Numbers 33:42-43.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית עֲבָדִים (beit avadim)
translationNotes.note: Not a general term for hardship. Exodus 1:11-14 describes forced labor gangs under taskmasters building the store cities Pithom and Rameses, working mortar and brick and the fields, and Exodus 5:7-19 records the quota of bricks held at the same figure after the straw was withheld and the workers were sent to gather stubble themselves.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses commands Israel to obey all his instructions so they may possess the promised land, reminding them how God sustained them in the wilderness for forty years to test their hearts. He warns that when they settle in the fertile land and grow wealthy, they must not forget God or credit their own strength, lest they turn to other gods and be destroyed like the nations before them.

stories.title: 📖 Deuteronomy 9
summaryBullets: Hear, O Israel: Today you are about to cross the Jordan to go in and dispossess nations greater and stronger than you, with large cities fortified to the heavens. (9:1).
The people are strong and tall, the descendants of the Anakim. You know about them, and you have heard it said, “Who can stand up to the sons of Anak?” (9:2).

But understand that today the LORD your God goes across ahead of you as a consuming fire; He will destroy them and subdue them before you. And you will drive them out and annihilate them swiftly, as the LORD has promised you. (9:3).

When the LORD your God has driven them out before you, do not say in your heart, “Because of my righteousness the LORD has brought me in to possess this land.” Rather, the LORD is driving out these nations before you because of their wickedness. (9:4).

It is not because of your righteousness or uprightness of heart that you are going in to possess their land, but it is because of their wickedness that the LORD your God is driving out these nations before you, to keep the promise He swore to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. (9:5).
Understand, then, that it is not because of your righteousness that the LORD your God is giving you this good land to possess, for you are a stiff-necked people. (9:6).

Remember this, and never forget how you provoked the LORD your God in the wilderness. From the day you left the land of Egypt until you reached this place, you have been rebelling against the LORD. (9:7).
At Horeb you provoked the LORD, and He was angry enough to destroy you. (9:8).

When I went up on the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I ate no bread and drank no water. (9:9).
Then the LORD gave me the two stone tablets, inscribed by the finger of God with the exact words that the LORD spoke to you out of the fire on the mountain on the day of the assembly. (9:10).
And at the end of forty days and forty nights, the LORD gave me the two stone tablets, the tablets of the covenant. (9:11).

And the LORD said to me, “Get up and go down from here at once, for your people, whom you brought out of Egypt, have corrupted themselves. How quickly they have turned aside from the way that I commanded them! They have made for themselves a molten image.” (9:12).
The LORD also said to me, “I have seen this people, and they are indeed a stiff-necked people. (9:13).
Leave Me alone, so that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. Then I will make you into a nation mightier and greater than they are.” (9:14).
So I went back down the mountain while it was blazing with fire, with the two tablets of the covenant in my hands. (9:15).
And I saw how you had sinned against the LORD your God; you had made for yourselves a molten calf. You had turned aside quickly from the way that the LORD had commanded you. (9:16).
So I took the two tablets and threw them out of my hands, shattering them before your eyes. (9:17).

Then I fell down before the LORD for forty days and forty nights, as I had done the first time. I did not eat bread or drink water because of all the sin you had committed in doing what was evil in the sight of the LORD and provoking Him to anger. (9:18).
For I was afraid of the anger and wrath that the LORD had directed against you, enough to destroy you. But the LORD listened to me this time as well. (9:19).
The LORD was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, but at that time I also prayed for Aaron. (9:20).

And I took that sinful thing, the calf you had made, and burned it in the fire. Then I crushed it and ground it to powder as fine as dust, and I cast it into the stream that came down from the mountain. (9:21).
You continued to provoke the LORD at Taberah, at Massah, and at Kibroth-hattaavah. (9:22).

And when the LORD sent you out from Kadesh-barnea, He said, “Go up and possess the land that I have given you.” But you rebelled against the command of the LORD your God. You neither believed Him nor obeyed Him. (9:23).
You have been rebelling against the LORD since the day I came to know you. (9:24).
So I fell down before the LORD for forty days and forty nights, because the LORD had said He would destroy you. (9:25).
And I prayed to the LORD and said, “O Lord GOD, do not destroy Your people, Your inheritance, whom You redeemed through Your greatness and brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand. (9:26).
Remember Your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Overlook the stubbornness of this people and the wickedness of their sin. (9:27).

Otherwise, those in the land from which You brought us out will say, ‘Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land He had promised them, and because He hated them, He has brought them out to kill them in the wilderness.’ (9:28).
But they are Your people, Your inheritance, whom You brought out by Your great power and outstretched arm.” (9:29).
crossRefs: Exodus 32:1-20: Israel makes the golden calf, and Moses breaks the tablets at the foot of the mountain.
Exodus 32:11-14: Moses pleads with God to relent, appealing to His own name and to the fathers.
Numbers 14:11-19: Moses makes the same plea after the spies, that Egypt not be able to say God could not bring them in.
Numbers 13:22-33: The Anakim of Hebron, the tall people no one can stand against.
Genesis 15:16: The land was not given sooner because the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet complete.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲנָקִים (Anaqim)
translationNotes.note: A people of unusual height living around Hebron in the southern hill country. The twelve men sent to scout the land came back naming three of them, Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, and reported that they felt like grasshoppers beside them (Numbers 13:22, 28, 33). Joshua 11:21-22 records Joshua cutting them out of the hill country, with survivors left only in the Philistine cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּצֻרֹת בַּשָּׁמַיִם (betsurot ba-shamayim)
translationNotes.note: Canaanite towns of this period sat on mounds built up from their own earlier ruins, ringed with a stone or mudbrick wall and often faced at the base with a glacis, a steep smooth slope of packed earth and plaster that kept a battering ram from reaching the wall and made undermining it impractical. An attacker on foot with no siege train was looking at exactly what the scouts described in Numbers 13:28.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קְשֵׁה־עֹרֶף (qesheh oref)
translationNotes.note: The picture is a plow animal that will not turn its neck to the rein or the goad. It is the standing charge against Israel from the golden calf onward (Exodus 32:9; 33:3, 5), and it is used again in verses 6 and 13 here. The neck is stiff against being steered, not merely proud.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵגֶל מַסֵּכָה (egel massekhah)
translationNotes.note: A massekhah is a cast metal image. Across Canaan and Egypt the bull stood for the strength of a god and often served as the pedestal the god was pictured standing on. Exodus 32:20 gives the same disposal recorded in verse 21: Moses burned it, ground it to powder, scattered it on the water, and made Israel drink it. Jeroboam later set up two golden calves at Bethel and Dan and repeated the words spoken at this one (1 Kings 12:28-29).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּבְעֵרָה (Taverah) - Hebrew: קִבְרוֹת הַתַּאֲוָה (Qivrot ha-Taavah)
translationNotes.note: Three of these names are verdicts. Taberah means burning, named where fire broke out at the edge of the camp (Numbers 11:1-3); Massah means testing, named where Israel demanded water and asked whether the LORD was among them (Exodus 17:7); Kibroth-hattaavah means graves of craving, named where the people who demanded meat were buried (Numbers 11:31-34). Kadesh-barnea is the oasis in the northern wilderness of Zin from which the twelve were sent up into the land (Numbers 13:26; 32:8).

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses tells Israel that though the nations ahead are strong, the Lord will drive them out because of those nations' wickedness, not Israel's righteousness; he then recounts how Israel made a golden calf at Horeb while he received the stone tablets, prompting him to break them, fast forty days, and intercede with the Lord to spare the people from destruction.

stories.title: 📖 Deuteronomy 10
summaryBullets: At that time the LORD said to me, “Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals, come up to Me on the mountain, and make an ark of wood. (10:1).
And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke; and you are to place them in the ark.” (10:2).
So I made an ark of acacia wood, chiseled out two stone tablets like the originals, and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hands. (10:3).

And the LORD wrote on the tablets what had been written previously, the Ten Commandments that He had spoken to you on the mountain out of the fire on the day of the assembly. The LORD gave them to me, (10:4).
and I went back down the mountain and placed the tablets in the ark I had made, as the LORD had commanded me; and there they have remained. (10:5).
The Israelites traveled from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah, where Aaron died and was buried, and Eleazar his son succeeded him as priest. (10:6).
From there they traveled to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land with streams of water. (10:7).

At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to stand before the LORD to serve Him, and to pronounce blessings in His name, as they do to this day. (10:8).
That is why Levi has no portion or inheritance among his brothers; the LORD is his inheritance, as the LORD your God promised him. (10:9).
I stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights, like the first time, and that time the LORD again listened to me and agreed not to destroy you. (10:10).
Then the LORD said to me, “Get up. Continue your journey ahead of the people, that they may enter and possess the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.” (10:11).

And now, O Israel, what does the LORD your God ask of you but to fear the LORD your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, (10:12).
and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD that I am giving you this day for your own good? (10:13).
Behold, to the LORD your God belong the heavens, even the highest heavens, and the earth and everything in it. (10:14).
Yet the LORD has set His affection on your fathers and loved them. And He has chosen you, their descendants after them, above all the peoples, even to this day. (10:15).
Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more. (10:16).
For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe. (10:17).
He executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing. (10:18).
So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt. (10:19).
You are to fear the LORD your God and serve Him. Hold fast to Him and take your oaths in His name. (10:20).
He is your praise and He is your God, who has done for you these great and awesome wonders that your eyes have seen. (10:21).
Your fathers went down to Egypt, seventy in all, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars in the sky. (10:22).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:1-4: Moses cuts two new stone tablets and carries them up the mountain at dawn.
Exodus 25:10-16: The ark is built of acacia wood to hold the testimony God gives Moses.
Numbers 3:5-10: The tribe of Levi is given to Aaron to do the service of the tabernacle.
Genesis 46:26-27: Seventy persons of Jacob's household went down into Egypt.
Deuteronomy 30:6: The LORD Himself will circumcise your heart, the promise standing behind the command in 10:16.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרוֹן (aron)
translationNotes.note: An aron is a chest or box, the same word used for Joseph's coffin in Genesis 50:26. Exodus 25:10-16 gives its size as two and a half cubits by one and a half by one and a half, roughly three and three quarter feet long by two and a quarter high and deep, made of acacia, overlaid inside and out with gold, and carried on poles that stayed in its rings. Acacia is the hard desert timber available in Sinai.

translationNotes.term: Levi has no portion or inheritance
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחֲלָה (nachalah)
translationNotes.note: Every other tribe received a block of land. Levi received none, and lived instead on the tithe of the other tribes (Numbers 18:21-24) and in forty-eight towns with their surrounding pasture, scattered through everyone else's territory (Numbers 35:1-8; Joshua 21). Verse 9 states the trade plainly: the LORD is his inheritance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָרְלַת לְבַבְכֶם (orlat levavkhem)
translationNotes.note: Literally the foreskin of your heart. Circumcision on the eighth day was the physical sign of the covenant cut with Abraham, and an uncircumcised male was to be cut off from his people (Genesis 17:10-14). Verse 16 applies the same operation to the inner man, as Deuteronomy 30:6 and Jeremiah 4:4 and 9:25-26 do.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֵּר (ger)
