translationNotes.note: A ger is a resident alien, someone living permanently in Israel who holds no clan land and therefore has no family to fall back on, which is why the law names him alongside the widow and the fatherless. He gleans the corners and the fallen fruit (Leviticus 19:9-10), rests on the sabbath (Exodus 20:10), stands under one law with the native-born (Leviticus 24:22), and may eat the Passover if circumcised (Exodus 12:48).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁבְעִים נֶפֶשׁ (shivim nephesh)
translationNotes.note: The figure comes from the household list in Genesis 46:8-27, repeated in Exodus 1:5. The Greek Septuagint reads seventy-five in both places, and that is the number Stephen gives when he retells the story in Acts 7:14.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses makes two new stone tablets, places them in an acacia ark, and spends forty days on the mountain where God rewrites the Ten Commandments; he then recounts the Levites' assignment to carry the ark, rehearses God's demand for obedience and love, and reminds Israel of their growth from seventy ancestors to a nation as numerous as the stars.

stories.title: 📖 Deuteronomy 11
summaryBullets: You shall therefore love the LORD your God and always keep His charge, His statutes, His ordinances, and His commandments. (11:1).
Know this day that it is not your children who have known and seen the discipline of the LORD your God: His greatness, His mighty hand, and His outstretched arm; (11:2).
the signs and works He did in Egypt to Pharaoh king of Egypt and all his land; (11:3).
what He did to the Egyptian army and horses and chariots when He made the waters of the Red Sea engulf them as they pursued you, and how He destroyed them completely, even to this day; (11:4).
what He did for you in the wilderness until you reached this place; (11:5).

and what He did in the midst of all the Israelites to Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab the Reubenite, when the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, their households, their tents, and every living thing that belonged to them. (11:6).
For it is your own eyes that have seen every great work that the LORD has done. (11:7).
You shall therefore keep every commandment I am giving you today, so that you may have the strength to go in and possess the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess, (11:8).
and so that you may live long in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give them and their descendants, a land flowing with milk and honey. (11:9).
For the land that you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated on foot, like a vegetable garden. (11:10).
But the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess is a land of mountains and valleys that drinks in the rain from heaven. (11:11).
It is a land for which the LORD your God cares; the eyes of the LORD your God are always on it, from the beginning to the end of the year. (11:12).
So if you carefully obey the commandments I am giving you today, to love the LORD your God and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul, (11:13).
then I will provide rain for your land in season, the autumn and spring rains, that you may gather your grain, new wine, and oil. (11:14).
And I will provide grass in the fields for your livestock, and you will eat and be satisfied. (11:15).
But be careful that you are not enticed to turn aside to worship and bow down to other gods, (11:16).

or the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you. He will shut the heavens so that there will be no rain, nor will the land yield its produce, and you will soon perish from the good land that the LORD is giving you. (11:17).
Fix these words of mine in your hearts and minds; tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. (11:18).
Teach them to your children, speaking about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. (11:19).
Write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates, (11:20).
so that as long as the heavens are above the earth, your days and those of your children may be multiplied in the land that the LORD swore to give your fathers. (11:21).
For if you carefully keep all these commandments I am giving you to follow— to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, and to hold fast to Him— (11:22).
then the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and stronger than you. (11:23).
Every place where the sole of your foot treads will be yours. Your territory will extend from the wilderness to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates River to the Western Sea. (11:24).
No man will be able to stand against you; the LORD your God will put the fear and dread of you upon all the land, wherever you set foot, as He has promised you. (11:25).
See, today I am setting before you a blessing and a curse — (11:26).
a blessing if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God that I am giving you today, (11:27).
but a curse if you disobey the commandments of the LORD your God and turn aside from the path I command you today by following other gods, which you have not known. (11:28).
When the LORD your God brings you into the land you are entering to possess, you are to proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. (11:29).
Are not these mountains across the Jordan, west of the road toward the sunset, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah opposite Gilgal near the Oak of Moreh? (11:30).
For you are about to cross the Jordan to enter and possess the land that the LORD your God is giving you. When you take possession of it and settle in it, (11:31).
be careful to follow all the statutes and ordinances that I am setting before you today. (11:32).
crossRefs: Numbers 16:31-33: The ground splits and swallows Dathan and Abiram alive, the event recalled in 11:6.
Deuteronomy 27:11-13: Six tribes are assigned to Gerizim for the blessing and six to Ebal for the curse.
Joshua 8:30-35: Joshua builds the altar on Mount Ebal and reads the blessings and the curses to all Israel.
Deuteronomy 6:6-9: The same command: these words on your heart, on your hand, on your doorposts.
1 Kings 17:1: Elijah shuts up the sky over Ahab, the drought this chapter holds over the land.

translationNotes.term: why the ceremony happens between two mountains
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁכֶם (Shekhem), Shechem, meaning shoulder
translationNotes.note: Gerizim and Ebal face each other across a narrow valley in the middle of the country, and the town of Shechem sits in the gap between them. That gap is the one easy east-west pass through the central hill country, and the main north-south ridge road runs through it too, so the ceremony was staged at the crossroads of the whole land rather than at its edge. Abram had built his first altar in Canaan at this same spot, by the Oak of Moreh, which Deuteronomy 11:30 names as the landmark (Genesis 12:6-7). Joshua 8:30-35 records the ceremony being carried out, half the people facing each mountain.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּתָן וַאֲבִירָם (Datan va-Aviram)
translationNotes.note: Verse 11:6 assumes the reader knows what happened, and Numbers 16 supplies it: two Reubenites joined Korah in challenging Moses' authority, and the ground opened and swallowed them, their households and everything they owned. Deuteronomy 11:6 lists it alongside the Red Sea as something this generation saw with their own eyes. Psalm 106:17 and Jude 1:11 both look back on it.

translationNotes.term: irrigated on foot like a vegetable garden
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְהִשְׁקִיתָ בְרַגְלְךָ (ve-hishqita ve-raglekha), 'and you watered with your foot'
translationNotes.note: Verses 11:10-11 contrast two farming systems. Egypt grew crops off the Nile flood and off canals, and water was moved by foot-worked lifting devices and by breaking small earth dams with the foot, so the phrase describes real equipment. Canaan has no such river; it is hill country that lives on rain, which is why 11:14 makes the rain itself the thing promised and 11:17 makes shutting the sky the thing threatened.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹרֶה וּמַלְקוֹשׁ (yoreh u-malqosh), the early and the latter rain
translationNotes.note: Two named rains, not a wet season. The yoreh falls in October and November and softens ground baked hard through the dry summer so it can be ploughed and sown; the malqosh falls in March and April and fills out the grain just before harvest. Miss either and the year fails. Jeremiah 5:24, Hosea 6:3, Joel 2:23 and James 5:7 all use the pair.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses tells Israel to love and obey God's commands, reminding them of what they witnessed in Egypt and the wilderness, and promises that faithfulness will bring rain and possession of the land while disobedience will bring drought and ruin. He instructs them to teach these words to their children and to recite blessings and curses at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal once they cross the Jordan.

stories.title: 🕍 Deuteronomy 12
summaryBullets: These are the statutes and ordinances you must be careful to follow all the days you live in the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess. (12:1).
Destroy completely all the places where the nations you are dispossessing have served their gods— atop the high mountains, on the hills, and under every green tree. (12:2).
Tear down their altars, smash their sacred pillars, burn up their Asherah poles, cut down the idols of their gods, and wipe out their names from every place. (12:3).
You shall not worship the LORD your God in this way. (12:4).
Instead, you must seek the place the LORD your God will choose from among all your tribes to establish as a dwelling for His Name, and there you must go. (12:5).

To that place you are to bring your burnt offerings and sacrifices, your tithes and heave offerings, your vow offerings and freewill offerings, as well as the firstborn of your herds and flocks. (12:6).
There, in the presence of the LORD your God, you and your households shall eat and rejoice in all you do, because the LORD your God has blessed you. (12:7).
You are not to do as we are doing here today, where everyone does what seems right in his own eyes. (12:8).
For you have not yet come to the resting place and the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you. (12:9).
When you cross the Jordan and live in the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, and He gives you rest from all the enemies around you and you dwell securely, (12:10).

then the LORD your God will choose a dwelling for His Name. And there you are to bring everything I command you: your burnt offerings and sacrifices, your tithes and special gifts, and all the choice offerings you vow to the LORD. (12:11).

And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God— you, your sons and daughters, your menservants and maidservants, and the Levite within your gates, since he has no portion or inheritance among you. (12:12).
Be careful not to offer your burnt offerings in just any place you see; (12:13).
you must offer them only in the place the LORD will choose in one of your tribal territories, and there you shall do all that I command you. (12:14).

But whenever you want, you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your gates, according to the blessing the LORD your God has given you. Both the ceremonially clean and unclean may eat it as they would a gazelle or deer, (12:15).
but you must not eat the blood; pour it on the ground like water. (12:16).

Within your gates you must not eat the tithe of your grain or new wine or oil, the firstborn of your herds or flocks, any of the offerings that you have vowed to give, or your freewill offerings or special gifts. (12:17).

Instead, you must eat them in the presence of the LORD your God at the place the LORD your God will choose— you, your sons and daughters, your menservants and maidservants, and the Levite within your gates. Rejoice before the LORD your God in all you do, (12:18).
and be careful not to neglect the Levites as long as you live in your land. (12:19).
When the LORD your God expands your territory as He has promised, and you crave meat and say, “I want to eat meat,” you may eat it whenever you want. (12:20).

If the place where the LORD your God chooses to put His Name is too far from you, then you may slaughter any of the herd or flock He has given you, as I have commanded you, and you may eat it within your gates whenever you want. (12:21).
Indeed, you may eat it as you would eat a gazelle or deer; both the ceremonially unclean and the clean may eat it. (12:22).
Only be sure not to eat the blood, because the blood is the life, and you must not eat the life with the meat. (12:23).
You must not eat the blood; pour it on the ground like water. (12:24).
Do not eat it, so that it may go well with you and your children after you, because you will be doing what is right in the eyes of the LORD. (12:25).
But you are to take your holy things and your vow offerings and go to the place the LORD will choose. (12:26).

Present the meat and blood of your burnt offerings on the altar of the LORD your God. The blood of your other sacrifices must be poured out beside the altar of the LORD your God, but you may eat the meat. (12:27).

Be careful to obey all these things I command you, so that it may always go well with you and your children after you, because you will be doing what is good and right in the eyes of the LORD your God. (12:28).
When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations you are entering to dispossess, and you drive them out and live in their land, (12:29).
be careful not to be ensnared by their ways after they have been destroyed before you. Do not inquire about their gods, asking, “How do these nations serve their gods? I will do likewise.” (12:30).

You must not worship the LORD your God in this way, because they practice for their gods every abomination which the LORD hates. They even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods. (12:31).
See that you do everything I command you; do not add to it or subtract from it. (12:32).
crossRefs: Leviticus 17:10-14: The prohibition on eating blood, because the life of the flesh is in the blood.
Numbers 33:52: Drive out the inhabitants, destroy their carved images and cast idols, and demolish their high places.
1 Kings 8:27-30: Solomon dedicates the temple as the place of which God said, My Name shall be there.
2 Kings 23:8-9: Josiah pulls down the high places and brings their priests in to Jerusalem.
John 4:20-24: The Samaritan woman asks which mountain is the place, and Jesus answers that the hour is coming.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲשֵׁרָה (ʾAsherah), Greek: Ἀστάρτη (Astarte), Aramaic: אשרה (Asherah)
translationNotes.note: Canaanite goddess; wooden poles or trees dedicated to her worship were to be cut down.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿăsēr), Greek: δεκάτη (dekátē), Aramaic: מעשרא (maʿsra)
translationNotes.note: A tenth of produce or livestock dedicated to God.

A male descendant of Levi (excluding the Aaronic priestly line). Assisted the priests in temple service: music, gatekeeping, instructing the people, preparing sacrifices. The priest and Levite who pass by the wounded man in the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:31-32) make Jesus' point cut sharper; both were professionally obligated to help.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֵוִי (lewi)

translationNotes.term: they even burn their sons and daughters
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֹלֶךְ (Molekh)
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 12:31 says outright what the worship of the nations included, and it is child sacrifice by fire. Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2-5 attach the death penalty to it under the name Molech, and 2 Kings 23:10 locates the site: the Topheth in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem. Two kings of Judah did it to their own sons, Ahaz and Manasseh (2 Kings 16:3, 21:6). The Greek form of that valley's name is Gehenna, the word translated hell in the New Testament.

translationNotes.term: high places, hills, and every green tree
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּמָה (bamah), a raised place
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 12:2 describes where Canaanite worship physically happened: on high mountains, on hills, and under spreading trees. A bamah was an open-air platform of stone with an altar on it, usually with a standing pillar and a wooden pole beside it, set on a ridge or beside a large tree rather than inside a roofed building. That is why the demolition orders in 12:3 come in a set of four: tear down the altars, smash the pillars, burn the poles, cut down the images.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses instructs Israel to destroy all pagan worship sites and bring sacrifices only to the place God chooses, while allowing slaughter of meat for eating in their own towns so long as they pour out the blood and avoid imitating the detestable practices of the nations they will dispossess.

stories.title: 🕍 Deuteronomy 13
summaryBullets: If a prophet or dreamer of dreams arises among you and proclaims a sign or wonder to you, (13:1).
and if the sign or wonder he has spoken to you comes about, but he says, “Let us follow other gods (which you have not known) and let us worship them,” (13:2).
you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer. For the LORD your God is testing you to find out whether you love Him with all your heart and with all your soul. (13:3).
You are to follow the LORD your God and fear Him. Keep His commandments and listen to His voice; serve Him and hold fast to Him. (13:4).

Such a prophet or dreamer must be put to death, because he has advocated rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery; he has tried to turn you from the way in which the LORD your God has commanded you to walk. So you must purge the evil from among you. (13:5).

If your very own brother, or your son or daughter, or the wife you embrace, or your closest friend secretly entices you, saying, “Let us go and worship other gods” (which neither you nor your fathers have known, (13:6).
the gods of the peoples around you, whether near or far, whether from one end of the earth or the other), (13:7).
you must not yield to him or listen to him. Show him no pity, and do not spare him or shield him. (13:8).
Instead, you must surely kill him. Your hand must be the first against him to put him to death, and then the hands of all the people. (13:9).
Stone him to death for trying to turn you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (13:10).
Then all Israel will hear and be afraid, and will never again do such a wicked thing among you. (13:11).
If, regarding one of the cities the LORD your God is giving you to inhabit, you hear it said (13:12).
that wicked men have arisen from among you and have led the people of their city astray, saying, “Let us go and serve other gods” (which you have not known), (13:13).
then you must inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly. And if it is established with certainty that this abomination has been committed among you, (13:14).
you must surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword. Devote to destruction all its people and livestock. (13:15).

And you are to gather all its plunder in the middle of the public square, and completely burn the city and all its plunder as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. The city must remain a mound of ruins forever, never to be rebuilt. (13:16).

Nothing devoted to destruction shall cling to your hands, so that the LORD will turn from His fierce anger, grant you mercy, show you compassion, and multiply you as He swore to your fathers, (13:17).
because you obey the LORD your God, keeping all His commandments I am giving you today and doing what is right in the eyes of the LORD your God. (13:18).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 18:20-22: A prophet who speaks presumptuously must die, and a word that does not come to pass was not from the LORD.
Jeremiah 23:16-22: Prophets who speak visions of their own minds and never stood in the council of the LORD.
Matthew 24:24: False christs and false prophets will perform great signs and wonders to lead astray.
Exodus 22:20: Whoever sacrifices to any god other than the LORD alone is to be devoted to destruction.
Joshua 7:24-26: Achan, his household, and everything devoted to destruction are destroyed in the Valley of Achor.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹת יוּמָת (mot yumat), 'he shall surely be put to death'
translationNotes.note: The chapter attaches this sentence to one crime, persuading Israel to serve other gods, and it applies it three ways: to a prophet whose sign comes true (13:5), to a family member who does it in private (13:9-10), and to a whole town (13:15). The procedure is not a lynching. Verse 13:14 requires that you inquire, investigate and interrogate thoroughly, and 17:6 fixes the evidence standard at two or three witnesses with never a conviction on one.

translationNotes.term: Purge the evil from your midst
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וּבִעַרְתָּ הָרָע מִקִּרְבֶּךָ (u-viarta ha-ra miqqirbekha)
translationNotes.note: A fixed closing formula on a completed case, used at 13:5, 17:7, 17:12, 19:19, 21:21, 22:21 and 24:7. The verb baar means to burn away or sweep out. It always follows a verdict and a stated procedure rather than standing on its own as a command to act, and Paul quotes the Greek of it at 1 Corinthians 5:13 when he tells the Corinthians to remove a man from the congregation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹת אוֹ מוֹפֵת (ot o mofet), a sign or a wonder
translationNotes.note: Verses 13:1-3 set a test that runs the other way from the one at 18:21-22. There, a prediction that fails marks a false prophet. Here the sign does come about, and the man is still to be rejected, because of what he says next: let us follow other gods. The chapter states the reason plainly at 13:3, that the LORD is testing whether Israel loves Him with all their heart.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת (ir hannidachat), 'the city that is led astray'
translationNotes.note: Verses 13:12-18 handle a whole town that has turned to other gods. The plunder is gathered in the public square and burned with the city as a whole burnt offering, nothing is taken, and the site is left a permanent ruin never to be rebuilt (13:16). Joshua 6:17-19 applies the same rule to Jericho, and Joshua 7 records Achan taking from the ban there and what followed.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses instructs Israel to execute any prophet or dreamer who performs signs but urges worship of other gods, and to put to death anyone - including family members - who secretly entices them to worship unknown gods; entire towns that turn to idolatry must be destroyed completely and burned as an offering to the LORD.

headings.text: Idolaters to Be Put to Death

stories.title: 🕍 Deuteronomy 14
summaryBullets: You are sons of the LORD your God; do not cut yourselves or shave your foreheads on behalf of the dead, (14:1).
for you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all the peoples on the face of the earth. (14:2).
You must not eat any detestable thing. (14:3).
These are the animals that you may eat: The ox, the sheep, the goat, (14:4).
the deer, the gazelle, the roe deer, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep. (14:5).
You may eat any animal that has a split hoof divided in two and that chews the cud. (14:6).

But of those that chew the cud or have a completely divided hoof, you are not to eat the following: the camel, the rabbit, or the rock badger. Although they chew the cud, they do not have a divided hoof. They are unclean for you, (14:7).
as well as the pig; though it has a divided hoof, it does not chew the cud. It is unclean for you. You must not eat its meat or touch its carcass. (14:8).
Of all the creatures that live in the water, you may eat anything with fins and scales, (14:9).
but you may not eat anything that does not have fins and scales; it is unclean for you. (14:10).
You may eat any clean bird, (14:11).
but these you may not eat: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture, (14:12).
the red kite, the falcon, any kind of kite, (14:13).
any kind of raven, (14:14).
the ostrich, the screech owl, the gull, any kind of hawk, (14:15).
the little owl, the great owl, the white owl, (14:16).
the desert owl, the osprey, the cormorant, (14:17).
the stork, any kind of heron, the hoopoe, or the bat. (14:18).
All flying insects are unclean for you; they may not be eaten. (14:19).
But you may eat any clean bird. (14:20).

You are not to eat any carcass; you may give it to the foreigner residing within your gates, and he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner. For you are a holy people belonging to the LORD your God. You must not cook a young goat in its mother’s milk. (14:21).
You must be sure to set aside a tenth of all the produce brought forth each year from your fields. (14:22).

And you are to eat a tenth of your grain, new wine, and oil, and the firstborn of your herds and flocks, in the presence of the LORD your God at the place He will choose as a dwelling for His Name, so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always. (14:23).
But if the distance is too great for you to carry that with which the LORD your God has blessed you, because the place where the LORD your God will choose to put His Name is too far away, (14:24).
then exchange it for money, take the money in your hand, and go to the place the LORD your God will choose. (14:25).

Then you may spend the money on anything you desire: cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink, or anything you wish. You are to feast there in the presence of the LORD your God and rejoice with your household. (14:26).
And do not neglect the Levite within your gates, since he has no portion or inheritance among you. (14:27).
At the end of every three years, bring a tenth of all your produce for that year and lay it up within your gates. (14:28).

Then the Levite (because he has no portion or inheritance among you), the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow within your gates may come and eat and be satisfied. And the LORD your God will bless you in all the work of your hands. (14:29).
crossRefs: Leviticus 11:1-47: The full list of clean and unclean creatures of land, water, air, and ground.
Numbers 18:21-24: The tithe is given to the Levites in return for their service, since they receive no land.
Deuteronomy 26:12-13: The declaration made before the LORD in the third year, when the tithe has been given away.
Malachi 3:10: Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in My house.
Acts 10:9-16: Peter's vision of the sheet let down with every kind of animal, and the voice telling him to kill and eat.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿăsēr), Greek: δεκάτη (dekátē), Aramaic: מעשרא (maʿsra)
translationNotes.note: A tenth of produce or livestock dedicated to God.

A male descendant of Levi (excluding the Aaronic priestly line). Assisted the priests in temple service: music, gatekeeping, instructing the people, preparing sacrifices. The priest and Levite who pass by the wounded man in the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:31-32) make Jesus' point cut sharper; both were professionally obligated to help.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֵוִי (lewi)

translationNotes.term: a young goat in its mother's milk
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גְּדִי בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ (gedi bachalev immo)
translationNotes.note: The command appears three times, at Exodus 23:19, Exodus 34:26, and here at Deuteronomy 14:21, and in the first two it is attached to the bringing of firstfruits, which points at a harvest rite rather than a recipe. Goat kids were slaughtered young and their mothers were in milk at the same season, so the raw material was to hand. Later Jewish practice built the whole separation of meat from dairy on this one sentence.

translationNotes.term: do not cut yourselves for the dead
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא תִתְגֹּדְדוּ (lo titgodedu), do not gash yourselves
translationNotes.note: Verses 14:1-2 forbid two mourning practices, cutting the body and shaving the front of the head bald, and give the reason in the same breath: you are sons of the LORD your God, a people holy to Him. Both were ordinary funeral customs among the surrounding peoples; 1 Kings 18:28 shows the prophets of Baal cutting themselves with swords and lances at Carmel, and Jeremiah 16:6 and 41:5 record the practice in the region. Leviticus 19:28 and 21:5 give the same ban.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses lists the animals Israel may and may not eat, prohibits eating anything already dead, and requires setting aside a tenth of annual produce to eat before the Lord at his chosen place; every three years the tithe is stored in towns to feed Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows.

stories.title: 🕍 Deuteronomy 15
summaryBullets: At the end of every seven years you must cancel debts. (15:1).

This is the manner of remission: Every creditor shall cancel what he has loaned to his neighbor. He is not to collect anything from his neighbor or brother, because the LORD’s time of release has been proclaimed. (15:2).
You may collect something from a foreigner, but you must forgive whatever your brother owes you. (15:3).
There will be no poor among you, however, because the LORD will surely bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess as an inheritance, (15:4).
if only you obey the LORD your God and are careful to follow all these commandments I am giving you today. (15:5).
When the LORD your God blesses you as He has promised, you will lend to many nations but borrow from none; you will rule over many nations but be ruled by none. (15:6).

If there is a poor man among your brothers within any of the gates in the land that the LORD your God is giving you, then you are not to harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother. (15:7).
Instead, you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs. (15:8).

Be careful not to harbor this wicked thought in your heart: “The seventh year, the year of release, is near,” so that you look upon your poor brother begrudgingly and give him nothing. He will cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin. (15:9).

Give generously to him, and do not let your heart be grieved when you do so. And because of this the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in everything to which you put your hand. (15:10).
For there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land. (15:11).
If a fellow Hebrew, a man or a woman, is sold to you and serves you six years, then in the seventh year you must set him free. (15:12).
And when you release him, do not send him away empty-handed. (15:13).
You are to furnish him liberally from your flock, your threshing floor, and your winepress. You shall give to him as the LORD your God has blessed you. (15:14).
Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; that is why I am giving you this command today. (15:15).
But if your servant says to you, ‘I do not want to leave you,’ because he loves you and your household and is well off with you, (15:16).
then take an awl and pierce it through his ear into the door, and he will become your servant for life. And treat your maidservant the same way. (15:17).
Do not regard it as a hardship to set your servant free, because his six years of service were worth twice the wages of a hired hand. And the LORD your God will bless you in all you do. (15:18).

You must set apart to the LORD your God every firstborn male produced by your herds and flocks. You are not to put the firstborn of your oxen to work, nor are you to shear the firstborn of your flock. (15:19).
Each year you and your household are to eat it before the LORD your God in the place the LORD will choose. (15:20).
But if an animal has a defect, is lame or blind, or has any serious flaw, you must not sacrifice it to the LORD your God. (15:21).
Eat it within your gates; both the ceremonially unclean and clean may eat it as they would a gazelle or a deer. (15:22).
But you must not eat the blood; pour it on the ground like water. (15:23).
crossRefs: Leviticus 25:1-7: In the seventh year the land keeps a sabbath, and the fields are neither sown nor reaped.
Exodus 21:2-6: A Hebrew servant serves six years and goes free, or has his ear pierced at the doorpost to stay for life.
Jeremiah 34:8-17: Judah frees its Hebrew slaves under this law, then takes them back, and God pronounces judgment.
Nehemiah 5:1-12: The nobles are made to cancel the debts and hand back the fields taken from their brothers.
Matthew 26:11: The poor you will always have with you, the same fact stated in 15:11.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁמִטָּה (shemittah), a letting drop or release
translationNotes.note: Shemittah is built on a verb meaning to let something fall out of your hand. Verses 15:1-3 apply it to debt: at the end of every seven years a creditor releases what he lent a fellow Israelite and may not collect it, though a loan to a foreigner still stands. Verse 15:9 names the obvious abuse and forbids it, refusing a loan because the seventh year is close. Exodus 23:10-11 and Leviticus 25:1-7 attach the same seventh year to the land, which is left unworked.

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּרֶן (goren)
Hebrew: עֶבֶד עִבְרִי (eved ivri), a Hebrew servant - חׇפְשִׁי (chophshi), free
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 15:12 covers an Israelite, man or woman, sold to pay a debt; it is not the purchase of a foreigner. Six years is the ceiling, and the seventh brings release whether the debt is cleared or not, the same term Exodus 21:2 sets. Verse 18 tells the owner not to resent it, on the ground that the six years were worth twice the wage of a hired man (mishneh sekhar sakhir). Jeremiah 34:8-17 records Judah obeying this law once and then taking the freed people back.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַעֲנֵיק תַּעֲנִיק (haaneiq taaniq), 'you shall surely furnish him'
translationNotes.note: Release alone was not enough; 15:13-14 forbids sending the man off empty-handed and names three stores he must be loaded from, the flock, the threshing floor, and the winepress. The verb is doubled in Hebrew for emphasis, and its root is the noun for a necklace or collar worn at the throat (Proverbs 1:9; Judges 8:26; Song of Songs 4:9), so the picture is a man sent away loaded rather than merely let go. Verse 15 gives the reason: you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD redeemed you.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַרְצֵעַ (martzea), a leatherworker's awl
translationNotes.note: A servant who refuses release says so, and his ear is driven through into the door with a punch; he then serves for life (15:16-17). Exodus 21:6 gives the same rite at the door or the doorpost. Deuteronomy adds a clause Exodus does not: 'And treat your maidservant the same way' (15:17). The mark is permanent and public, which is why it goes on the ear at the doorway of the house he chose.

translationNotes.term: The firstborn of herd and flock
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּכוֹר (bekhor), firstborn
translationNotes.note: Every firstborn male of the herd and flock is set apart to the LORD, and 15:19 bars the owner from working the ox or shearing the sheep, so he draws no labor and no wool from it. It is eaten yearly before the LORD at the place He chooses (15:20). An animal that is lame, blind, or otherwise flawed is disqualified from the altar and is eaten at home instead, by clean and unclean alike, like a gazelle or a deer (15:21-22). The claim on the firstborn goes back to the exodus itself, Exodus 13:11-15.

stories.keyTakeaway: Every seven years Israelites must cancel debts owed by fellow Israelites, remain generous to the poor, release Hebrew servants after six years with provisions, and set apart firstborn male animals for annual feasts before the LORD.

stories.title: 🕍 Deuteronomy 16
summaryBullets: Observe the month of Abib and celebrate the Passover to the LORD your God, because in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night. (16:1).
You are to offer to the LORD your God the Passover sacrifice from the herd or flock in the place the LORD will choose as a dwelling for His Name. (16:2).

You must not eat leavened bread with it; for seven days you are to eat with it unleavened bread, the bread of affliction, because you left the land of Egypt in haste— so that you may remember for the rest of your life the day you left the land of Egypt. (16:3).
No leaven is to be found in all your land for seven days, and none of the meat you sacrifice in the evening of the first day shall remain until morning. (16:4).
You are not to sacrifice the Passover animal in any of the towns that the LORD your God is giving you. (16:5).

You must only offer the Passover sacrifice at the place the LORD your God will choose as a dwelling for His Name. Do this in the evening as the sun sets, at the same time you departed from Egypt. (16:6).
And you shall roast it and eat it in the place the LORD your God will choose, and in the morning you shall return to your tents. (16:7).
For six days you must eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day you shall hold a solemn assembly to the LORD your God, and you must not do any work. (16:8).
You are to count off seven weeks from the time you first put the sickle to the standing grain. (16:9).
And you shall celebrate the Feast of Weeks to the LORD your God with a freewill offering that you give in proportion to how the LORD your God has blessed you, (16:10).

and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God in the place He will choose as a dwelling for His Name — you, your sons and daughters, your menservants and maidservants, and the Levite within your gates, as well as the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widows among you. (16:11).
Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and carefully follow these statutes. (16:12).
You are to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles for seven days after you have gathered the produce of your threshing floor and your winepress. (16:13).
And you shall rejoice in your feast— you, your sons and daughters, your menservants and maidservants, and the Levite, as well as the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widows among you. (16:14).

For seven days you shall celebrate a feast to the LORD your God in the place He will choose, because the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that your joy will be complete. (16:15).

Three times a year all your men are to appear before the LORD your God in the place He will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles. No one should appear before the LORD empty-handed. (16:16).
Everyone must appear with a gift as he is able, according to the blessing the LORD your God has given you. (16:17).
You are to appoint judges and officials for your tribes in every town that the LORD your God is giving you. They are to judge the people with righteous judgment. (16:18).
Do not deny justice or show partiality. Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous. (16:19).
Pursue justice, and justice alone, so that you may live, and you may possess the land that the LORD your God is giving you. (16:20).
Do not set up any wooden Asherah pole next to the altar you will build for the LORD your God, (16:21).
and do not set up for yourselves a sacred pillar, which the LORD your God hates. (16:22).
crossRefs: Exodus 12:1-14: The first Passover, the lamb taken on the tenth day and the blood put on the doorframes.
Leviticus 23:4-44: The full calendar of appointed times, from Passover through Weeks to Booths.
Exodus 23:14-17: Three times a year every male is to appear before the Lord GOD.
Acts 2:1-4: The Feast of Weeks, called Pentecost, when the sound of wind fills the house.
John 7:37-38: On the last and greatest day of the Feast of Booths, Jesus stands and calls the thirsty to come to Him.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲשֵׁרָה (ʾAsherah), Greek: Ἀστάρτη (Astarte), Aramaic: אשרה (Asherah)
translationNotes.note: Canaanite goddess; wooden poles or trees dedicated to her worship were to be cut down.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת (Chag ha-Sukkot), the Feast of Shelters
translationNotes.note: The third of the three pilgrim feasts, kept for seven days after the grain is in from the threshing floor and the grapes are pressed (16:13). A sukkah is a rough branch shelter of the kind thrown up in a field at harvest, and Leviticus 23:42-43 orders Israel to live in them so each generation would know their fathers did on the way out of Egypt. Deuteronomy 31:10-13 attaches a public reading of the whole law to this feast every seventh year.

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּרֶן (goren)

translationNotes.note: A male descendant of Levi (excluding the Aaronic priestly line). Assisted the priests in temple service: music, gatekeeping, instructing the people, preparing sacrifices. The priest and Levite who pass by the wounded man in the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:31-32) make Jesus' point cut sharper; both were professionally obligated to help.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֵוִי (lewi)

translationNotes.term: judges and officers in all your gates
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁפְטִים וְשֹׁטְרִים (shofetim ve-shoterim)
translationNotes.note: Verse 16:18 puts a court in every town, in the gate. A gate in a walled town was a chambered structure with benches, the one covered public space where business was witnessed and disputes were heard; excavated gates at Gezer, Hazor and Megiddo show the side rooms. That is why Boaz takes his case to the gate and seats ten elders there (Ruth 4:1-2). Verses 16:19-20 give the standing rules: no partiality, no bribes, because a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses prescribes three annual festivals - Passover, Weeks, and Tabernacles - to be celebrated at the place God chooses, with instructions to eat unleavened bread, give freewill offerings, and include servants and foreigners in the rejoicing. He also commands the appointment of judges in every town to administer justice fairly and prohibits setting up Asherah poles or sacred stones.

headings.text: Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread

stories.title: ⚖️ Deuteronomy 17
summaryBullets: You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep with any defect or serious flaw, for that is detestable to the LORD your God. (17:1).
If a man or woman among you in one of the towns that the LORD your God gives you is found doing evil in the sight of the LORD your God by transgressing His covenant (17:2).
and going to worship other gods, bowing down to them or to the sun or moon or any of the host of heaven— which I have forbidden— (17:3).
and if it is reported and you hear about it, you must investigate it thoroughly. If the report is true and such an abomination has happened in Israel, (17:4).
you must bring out to your gates the man or woman who has done this evil thing, and you must stone that person to death. (17:5).
On the testimony of two or three witnesses a man shall be put to death, but he shall not be executed on the testimony of a lone witness. (17:6).
The hands of the witnesses shall be the first in putting him to death, and after that, the hands of all the people. So you must purge the evil from among you. (17:7).

If a case is too difficult for you to judge, whether the controversy within your gates is regarding bloodshed, lawsuits, or assaults, you must go up to the place the LORD your God will choose. (17:8).
You are to go to the Levitical priests and to the judge who presides at that time. Inquire of them, and they will give you a verdict in the case. (17:9).
You must abide by the verdict they give you at the place the LORD will choose. Be careful to do everything they instruct you, (17:10).
according to the terms of law they give and the verdict they proclaim. Do not turn aside to the right or to the left from the decision they declare to you. (17:11).

But the man who acts presumptuously, refusing to listen either to the priest who stands there to serve the LORD your God, or to the judge, must be put to death. You must purge the evil from Israel. (17:12).
Then all the people will hear and be afraid, and will no longer behave arrogantly. (17:13).
When you enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you and have taken possession of it and settled in it, and you say, “Let us set a king over us like all the nations around us,” (17:14).

you are to appoint over yourselves the king whom the LORD your God shall choose. Appoint a king from among your brothers; you are not to set over yourselves a foreigner who is not one of your brothers. (17:15).
But the king must not acquire many horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to acquire more horses, for the LORD has said, ‘You are never to go back that way again.’ (17:16).
He must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray. He must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold. (17:17).
When he is seated on his royal throne, he must write for himself a copy of this instruction on a scroll in the presence of the Levitical priests. (17:18).

It is to remain with him, and he is to read from it all the days of his life, so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by carefully observing all the words of this instruction and these statutes. (17:19).

Then his heart will not be exalted above his countrymen, and he will not turn aside from the commandment, to the right or to the left, in order that he and his sons may reign many years over his kingdom in Israel. (17:20).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 8:4-22: Israel demands a king like the other nations, and Samuel spells out what a king will take from them.
1 Kings 10:26-29: Solomon accumulates chariots and horses and has them imported out of Egypt.
1 Kings 11:1-4: Solomon's wives are many and foreign, and in his old age they turn his heart away.
Numbers 35:30: No one is put to death on the testimony of a single witness.
2 Chronicles 19:8-11: Jehoshaphat sets Levites, priests, and family heads in Jerusalem to decide the hard cases.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא־יַרְבֶּה (lo yarbeh), he shall not multiply
translationNotes.note: Three bans, and each one names a thing every king around Israel actually did. Chariot horses were the ancient equivalent of armor, bought abroad and stockpiled. Wives were treaty instruments, because a foreign king sealed an alliance by sending a daughter. Silver and gold were taken as tribute and hoarded. Solomon broke all three: 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses imported from Egypt and Kue (1 Kings 10:26-29), silver made as common as stones, and seven hundred wives of royal birth plus three hundred concubines who turned his heart (1 Kings 11:1-3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁנֵה הַתּוֹרָה (mishneh hattorah) - Greek: Δευτερονόμιον (Deuteronomion)
translationNotes.note: The king was to write out the law in his own hand, in front of the priests, and read it his whole life (17:18-19). The Hebrew phrase for what he copies is mishneh hattorah, a repetition or second copy of the instruction. When the Old Testament was translated into Greek, that phrase was rendered deuteronomion, second law, and the name stuck to the whole book. That is where the English title Deuteronomy comes from.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יַד הָעֵדִים תִּהְיֶה־בּוֹ בָרִאשֹׁנָה (yad ha-edim tihyeh-bo varishonah)
translationNotes.note: Verse 17:7 puts the hands of the witnesses first in carrying out an execution, and the whole assembly after them. The rule makes the men whose testimony convicted a man do the killing themselves, and 19:16-21 sets the penalty for false witness at whatever the liar intended for his brother. Verse 17:6 fixes the standard at two or three witnesses and rules out conviction on one; John 8:7 turns on the same procedure.

translationNotes.term: a case too difficult to judge
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּי יִפָּלֵא מִמְּךָ דָבָר (ki yippale mimmekha davar)
translationNotes.note: Verses 17:8-13 build an appeal court. A local gate court that cannot settle a case of bloodshed, a lawsuit or an assault sends it up to the priests and the presiding judge at the central sanctuary, whose verdict is binding, and refusing it is a capital matter. 2 Chronicles 19:8-11 records Jehoshaphat setting up exactly this court in Jerusalem with Levites, priests and heads of families, and dividing it between matters of the LORD and matters of the king.

stories.keyTakeaway: Sacrifices must be unblemished; those who worship other gods are to be stoned to death on testimony of two or three witnesses, with the witnesses throwing the first stones. Difficult legal cases go to the Levitical priests and judge for verdict; when Israel appoints a king, he must be an Israelite chosen by God, avoid acquiring horses and wives and wealth, and copy and read the law daily to remain humble.

stories.title: ⚖️ Deuteronomy 18
summaryBullets: The Levitical priests — indeed the whole tribe of Levi — shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They are to eat the food offerings to the LORD; that is their inheritance. (18:1).
Although they have no inheritance among their brothers, the LORD is their inheritance, as He promised them. (18:2).
This shall be the priests’ share from the people who offer a sacrifice, whether a bull or a sheep: the priests are to be given the shoulder, the jowls, and the stomach. (18:3).
You are to give them the firstfruits of your grain, new wine, and oil, and the first wool sheared from your flock. (18:4).
For the LORD your God has chosen Levi and his sons out of all your tribes to stand and minister in His name for all time. (18:5).
Now if a Levite moves from any town of residence throughout Israel and comes in all earnestness to the place the LORD will choose, (18:6).
then he shall serve in the name of the LORD his God like all his fellow Levites who stand there before the LORD. (18:7).
They shall eat equal portions, even though he has received money from the sale of his father’s estate. (18:8).
When you enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you, do not imitate the detestable ways of the nations there. (18:9).
Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery, (18:10).
casts spells, consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead. (18:11).
For whoever does these things is detestable to the LORD. And because of these detestable things, the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you. (18:12).
You must be blameless before the LORD your God. (18:13).
Though these nations, which you will dispossess, listen to conjurers and diviners, the LORD your God has not permitted you to do so. (18:14).
The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him. (18:15).

This is what you asked of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, “Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!” (18:16).
Then the LORD said to me, “They have spoken well. (18:17).
I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him. (18:18).
And I will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to My words that the prophet speaks in My name. (18:19).
But if any prophet dares to speak a message in My name that I have not commanded him to speak, or to speak in the name of other gods, that prophet must be put to death.” (18:20).
You may ask in your heart, “How can we recognize a message that the LORD has not spoken?” (18:21).

When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken. The prophet has spoken presumptuously. Do not be afraid of him. (18:22).
crossRefs: Numbers 18:8-20: The offerings assigned to the priests, since the LORD Himself is their portion and inheritance.
Leviticus 20:27: A man or woman who is a medium or a spiritist is to be put to death.
1 Samuel 28:7-19: Saul goes by night to the medium at Endor, doing the very thing forbidden here.
Acts 3:22-23: Peter applies the promise of a prophet like Moses to Jesus, and warns that whoever will not listen is cut off.
John 1:19-25: The priests and Levites ask John the Baptist whether he is the Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָבִיא (navi) - Greek: προφήτης (prophetes)
translationNotes.note: A navi speaks for someone else; Exodus 7:1 makes the relation plain by calling Aaron Moses' navi. The office is not fortune-telling, which is what 18:10-14 has just banned, and 18:21-22 gives the one test the reader can apply: what he says in the LORD's name either happens or it does not. Verse 18:15 promises a prophet like Moses from among Israel's own brothers, which Peter quotes at Acts 3:22 and Stephen at Acts 7:37.

The first portion of each harvest offered to God before the rest could be eaten (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:9-14). Paul calls the resurrected Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20); the guarantee that the full resurrection harvest will follow.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּכּוּרִים (bikkurim)

translationNotes.note: A male descendant of Levi (excluding the Aaronic priestly line). Assisted the priests in temple service: music, gatekeeping, instructing the people, preparing sacrifices. The priest and Levite who pass by the wounded man in the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:31-32) make Jesus' point cut sharper; both were professionally obligated to help.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֵוִי (lewi)
Hebrew: קֹסֵם קְסָמִים (qosem qesamim), diviner - מְעוֹנֵן (meonen) - מְנַחֵשׁ (menachesh) - מְכַשֵּׁף (mekhashef)
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 18:10-11 gives the fullest list in Scripture of the occult trades, eight of them, on top of child sacrifice: the diviner who reads the future for a fee, the soothsayer, the reader of omens, the sorcerer, the caster of spells, the one who consults a medium, the spiritist, and the one who inquires of the dead. These were licensed professions with royal patronage in Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt, paid to read the livers of sacrificed animals, the flight of birds, the movements of stars, and dreams. Israel was to have none of them; verse 15 puts a prophet in their place.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דֹּרֵשׁ אֶל־הַמֵּתִים (doresh el-hametim)
translationNotes.note: Necromancy was the attempt to get answers from a dead person through a practitioner. Scripture records exactly one case in detail: Saul, who had himself expelled the mediums, went in disguise to a woman at En-dor the night before his last battle and asked her to bring up Samuel (1 Samuel 28:3-20). Leviticus 20:27 sets death for the practitioner and 1 Chronicles 10:13 names this consultation as part of why Saul died.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses establishes that the Levites receive food offerings instead of land inheritance, prohibits Israel from practicing divination and child sacrifice like the nations they will displace, and announces that God will raise up a prophet like Moses whom Israel must obey; false prophets are to be executed.

stories.title: ⚖️ Deuteronomy 19
summaryBullets: When the LORD your God has cut off the nations whose land He is giving you, and when you have driven them out and settled in their cities and houses, (19:1).
then you are to set apart for yourselves three cities within the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess. (19:2).
You are to build roads for yourselves and divide into three regions the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, so that any manslayer can flee to these cities. (19:3).
Now this is the situation regarding the manslayer who flees to one of these cities to save his life, having killed his neighbor accidentally, without intending to harm him: (19:4).

If he goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut timber and swings his axe to chop down a tree, but the blade flies off the handle and strikes and kills his neighbor, he may flee to one of these cities to save his life. (19:5).

Otherwise, the avenger of blood might pursue the manslayer in a rage, overtake him if the distance is great, and strike him dead though he did not deserve to die, since he did not intend any harm. (19:6).
This is why I am commanding you to set apart for yourselves three cities. (19:7).
And if the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as He swore to your fathers, and gives you all the land He promised them, (19:8).
and if you carefully keep all these commandments I am giving you today, loving the LORD your God and walking in His ways at all times, then you are to add three more cities to these three. (19:9).
Thus innocent blood will not be shed in the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, so that you will not be guilty of bloodshed. (19:10).
If, however, a man hates his neighbor and lies in wait, attacks him and kills him, and then flees to one of these cities, (19:11).
the elders of his city must send for him, bring him back, and hand him over to the avenger of blood to die. (19:12).
You must show him no pity. You are to purge from Israel the guilt of shedding innocent blood, that it may go well with you. (19:13).
You must not move your neighbor’s boundary marker, which was set up by your ancestors to mark the inheritance you shall receive in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess. (19:14).

A lone witness is not sufficient to establish any wrongdoing or sin against a man, regardless of what offense he may have committed. A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. (19:15).
If a false witness testifies against someone, accusing him of a crime, (19:16).
both parties to the dispute must stand in the presence of the LORD, before the priests and judges who are in office at that time. (19:17).
The judges shall investigate thoroughly, and if the witness is proven to be a liar who has falsely accused his brother, (19:18).
you must do to him as he intended to do to his brother. So you must purge the evil from among you. (19:19).
Then the rest of the people will hear and be afraid, and they will never again do anything so evil among you. (19:20).
You must show no pity: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, and foot for foot. (19:21).
crossRefs: Numbers 35:9-28: The full law of the cities of refuge, where the congregation judges between the killer and the avenger of blood and no one is put to death on the word of a lone witness.
Leviticus 19:18: The same law forbids seeking revenge and bearing a grudge against your own people, which is why 19:21 is a sentence for judges to pass rather than a licence to settle a score.
Deuteronomy 32:35: 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' says the LORD in Moses' own song, thirteen chapters after the eye-for-eye standard is handed to the judges here.
Exodus 21:22-25: The same list of life for life and eye for eye given at Sinai, where 21:22 has the penalty assessed as the court allows.

Matthew 5:38-39: Jesus quotes 'Eye for eye and tooth for tooth' and tells each hearer not to resist an evil person but to turn the other cheek, addressing the man who has been struck rather than the bench.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָבִיא (nābîʾ), Greek: προφήτης (prophētēs), Aramaic: נביא (navi)
translationNotes.note: A spokesperson who declares God’s message, not their own.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֶסֶם (qesem), Greek: μαντεία (manteia), Aramaic: קסמא (qisma)
translationNotes.note: Attempting to predict or control events through occult means; forbidden as abomination.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָרֵי מִקְלָט (ʿarei miqlat), Greek: πόλεις καταφυγῆς (poleis kataphygēs), Aramaic: קרי מקלטא (qarei miqlata)
translationNotes.note: Designated towns where those guilty of unintentional manslaughter could seek asylum.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵרֶם (ḥerem), Greek: ἀνάθεμα (anathema), Aramaic: חרמא (ḥerma)
translationNotes.note: To set apart for total annihilation; complete removal from human use in obedience to God’s command.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּאֵל הַדָּם (goel ha-dam), the redeemer of blood
translationNotes.note: There was no police force and no public prosecutor. When a man was killed, the duty of answering for it fell on his nearest male relative, the goel, and the same word names the kinsman who buys back family land or marries a childless widow, which is the role Boaz takes in Ruth 3 and 4. Deuteronomy 19:6 pictures him giving chase in a rage while the trail is hot. The cities of refuge exist to interrupt that chase and put a trial in its place: Numbers 35:24-25 has the assembly judge between the killer and the avenger, and the manslayer then stays in the city until the death of the high priest.

translationNotes.term: the axe head flies off the handle
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁגֵג (shogeg), acting in error
translationNotes.note: The law does not deal in abstractions; it gives a working case. Two men go into the woods to cut timber, the iron head comes loose off the wooden helve mid-swing, and the other man is dead (19:5). Iron tools were fitted by wedging the head onto a shaped haft, so a head coming off was a common accident; 2 Kings 6:5 has one fly into the Jordan. That is the test case for what counts as killing without intent, set against 19:11 where a man lies in wait first.

translationNotes.term: the six cities and where they stood
translationNotes.note: Joshua 20:7-8 names the finished set. West of the Jordan: Kedesh in Galilee up north, Shechem in the Ephraim hill country in the middle, and Hebron in Judah in the south. East of the Jordan: Golan in Bashan, Ramoth in Gilead, and Bezer on the wilderness plateau. Three and three, spread north to south on both sides of the river, which is what Deuteronomy 19:3 means by dividing the land in three and building roads.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹצֵחַ (rotseach), one who takes a life, covering both cases - בִּשְׁגָגָה (bishgagah), unintentionally - שֹׁגֵג (shogeg), acting in error
translationNotes.note: Hebrew does not have one word for murderer and a second for manslayer. Rotseach covers both, and Numbers 35:11 uses it of the man who kills bishgagah, unintentionally, the very man the city of refuge is built to protect; 35:25 uses it again of the man the congregation rescues from the avenger. English 'homicide' has the same range. What separates the two cases is not the noun but the evidence, and Deuteronomy 19:4-6 gives the test: whether the killer hated the man beforehand. Numbers 35:16-23 lists the marks of each.

translationNotes.term: Eye for eye as a ceiling
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶפֶשׁ בְּנֶפֶשׁ עַיִן בְּעַיִן (nefesh benefesh ayin beayin), 'life for life, eye for eye'
translationNotes.note: The formula caps a penalty; it does not license one. The measure of what may be done to the offender is exactly the harm he caused and no more, which is the point of the matching pairs at 19:21 and of Leviticus 24:19-20, 'as he has done, so shall it be done to him.' The same wording appears in Babylon and is graded by rank: the laws of Hammurabi take an eye for an eye between men of standing (law 196) but settle the eye of a freed man with a mina of silver (198) and the eye of a slave at half his price (199). Leviticus 24:22 sets one standard for the foreigner and the native alike.

translationNotes.term: The penalty falls on the false witness
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵד חָמָס (ed chamas), a malicious witness
translationNotes.note: Eye for eye in this chapter is not a rule about injuries at all. It sits at the end of 19:16-21, the case of a man who testifies falsely to destroy someone: the judges investigate, and 19:19 orders that they do to him what he intended to do to his brother. In a capital charge that means his own life. The measure that caps the penalty is the harm he tried to cause, and 19:15 requires two or three witnesses before any charge stands at all, which Deuteronomy 17:6 repeats for capital cases.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel must designate three cities of refuge where someone who kills unintentionally can escape vengeance, but premeditated murderers will be executed; additionally, disputes require two or three witnesses, false witnesses receive the punishment they intended for others, and boundary stones must not be moved.

headings.text: The Testimony of Two or Three Witnesses

stories.title: ⚖️ Deuteronomy 20
summaryBullets: When you go out to war against your enemies and see horses, chariots, and an army larger than yours, do not be afraid of them; for the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you. (20:1).
When you are about to go into battle, the priest is to come forward and address the army, (20:2).
saying to them, “Hear, O Israel, today you are going into battle with your enemies. Do not be fainthearted or afraid; do not be alarmed or terrified because of them. (20:3).
For the LORD your God goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.” (20:4).
Furthermore, the officers are to address the army, saying, “Has any man built a new house and not dedicated it? Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man dedicate it. (20:5).
Has any man planted a vineyard and not begun to enjoy its fruit? Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man enjoy its fruit. (20:6).
Has any man become pledged to a woman and not married her? Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man marry her.” (20:7).
Then the officers shall speak further to the army, saying, “Is any man afraid or fainthearted? Let him return home, so that the hearts of his brothers will not melt like his own.” (20:8).
When the officers have finished addressing the army, they are to appoint commanders to lead it. (20:9).
When you approach a city to fight against it, you are to make an offer of peace. (20:10).
If they accept your offer of peace and open their gates, all the people there will become forced laborers to serve you. (20:11).
But if they refuse to make peace with you and wage war against you, lay siege to that city. (20:12).
When the LORD your God has delivered it into your hand, you must put every male to the sword. (20:13).
But the women, children, livestock, and whatever else is in the city— all its spoil— you may take as plunder, and you shall use the spoil of your enemies that the LORD your God gives you. (20:14).
This is how you are to treat all the cities that are far away from you and do not belong to the nations nearby. (20:15).
However, in the cities of the nations that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, you must not leave alive anything that breathes. (20:16).
For you must devote them to complete destruction— the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites— as the LORD your God has commanded you, (20:17).
so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods, and so cause you to sin against the LORD your God. (20:18).

When you lay siege to a city for an extended time while fighting against it to capture it, you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit. You must not cut them down. Are the trees of the field human, that you should besiege them? (20:19).
But you may destroy the trees that you know do not produce fruit. Use them to build siege works against the city that is waging war against you, until it falls. (20:20).
crossRefs: Genesis 15:16: God tells Abram his descendants will not come back for four generations because 'the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete', so the land is not taken until the case against its inhabitants is full.

Deuteronomy 9:4-5: Israel is told twice in two verses not to say the land is theirs for their own righteousness; it is the wickedness of these nations and the promise sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Leviticus 18:24-28: The practices that defiled the land are listed, and Israel is warned in the same breath that the land will vomit them out too if they do the same, which puts both under one standard.
Joshua 6:20-25: Jericho falls and everything in it is devoted to destruction, and in the same account Rahab and her whole household are brought out alive.

Joshua 9:15-27: The Gibeonites pose as travellers from a distant country, Israel swears an oath to them, and the leaders keep it, so the Gibeonites live on among Israel as woodcutters and water carriers.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵרֶם (cherem)
translationNotes.note: Cherem puts something permanently beyond ordinary use by handing it to God, and Leviticus 27:28-29 says what is placed under it cannot be redeemed or sold. Deuteronomy 20 divides its targets: cities far off are offered terms of peace first, and if they refuse and are taken, the women, children and livestock are kept (20:10-15). The cherem is applied only to the six named peoples of the land at 20:16-18, and 20:18 gives the stated reason, that they would teach Israel their practices.

translationNotes.term: who is sent home before the battle
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁטְרִים (shoterim), officers
translationNotes.note: Before the fighting, four groups are released: the man who has built a house and not yet dedicated it, the man who has planted a vineyard and not yet eaten from it, the man betrothed but not yet married, and any man who is afraid (20:5-8). A vineyard takes four or five years to come into use under Leviticus 19:23-25, so the second exemption covers years of work. No other army in the ancient world is known to have discharged its frightened men on request and given the reason as morale.

translationNotes.term: do not put an axe to the fruit trees
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵץ הַשָּׂדֶה (ets hasadeh), the tree of the field
translationNotes.note: Cutting down an enemy's orchards was standard siege practice; Assyrian royal inscriptions boast of felling groves and wrecking irrigation to break a region for a generation. Deuteronomy 20:19-20 forbids it for fruit trees and permits it only for trees that bear nothing, which may be cut for siege works. An olive tree takes decades to come into full bearing, so the rule protects the people who will live there after the war.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְקָרָאתָ אֵלֶיהָ לְשָׁלוֹם (ve-qarata eleha le-shalom)
translationNotes.note: Verse 20:10 requires a formal offer before any siege of a distant city, and 20:11 sets the outcome if it is accepted, that the population becomes a labour force rather than a casualty list. Verses 20:5-8 have already sent four groups home before the fighting: the man with a new house not yet dedicated, the man with a new vineyard he has not eaten from, the man betrothed but not married, and anyone who is afraid. Judges 7:3 shows Gideon applying the last of those.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses instructs Israel on warfare: trust God's presence in battle, allow certain men to return home before fighting, offer peace to distant cities and enslave those who surrender, completely destroy the nearby Canaanite nations, and preserve fruit trees during sieges.

stories.title: ⚖️ Deuteronomy 21
summaryBullets: If one is found slain, lying in a field in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess, and it is not known who killed him, (21:1).
your elders and judges must come out and measure the distance from the victim to the neighboring cities. (21:2).
Then the elders of the city nearest the victim shall take a heifer that has never been yoked or used for work, (21:3).
bring the heifer to a valley with running water that has not been plowed or sown, and break its neck there by the stream. (21:4).

And the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward, for the LORD your God has chosen them to serve Him and pronounce blessings in His name and to give a ruling in every dispute and case of assault. (21:5).
Then all the elders of the city nearest the victim shall wash their hands by the stream over the heifer whose neck has been broken, (21:6).
and they shall declare, “Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it. (21:7).
Accept this atonement, O LORD, for Your people Israel whom You have redeemed, and do not hold the shedding of innocent blood against them.” And the bloodshed will be atoned for. (21:8).
So you shall purge from among you the guilt of shedding innocent blood, since you have done what is right in the eyes of the LORD. (21:9).
When you go to war against your enemies and the LORD your God delivers them into your hand and you take them captive, (21:10).
if you see a beautiful woman among them, and you desire her and want to take her as your wife, (21:11).
then you shall bring her into your house. She must shave her head, trim her nails, (21:12).

and put aside the clothing of her captivity. After she has lived in your house a full month and mourned her father and mother, you may have relations with her and be her husband, and she shall be your wife. (21:13).
And if you are not pleased with her, you are to let her go wherever she wishes. But you must not sell her for money or treat her as a slave, since you have dishonored her. (21:14).
If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other unloved, and both bear him sons, but the unloved wife has the firstborn son, (21:15).
when that man assigns his inheritance to his sons he must not appoint the son of the beloved wife as the firstborn over the son of the unloved wife. (21:16).

Instead, he must acknowledge the firstborn, the son of his unloved wife, by giving him a double portion of all that he has. For that son is the firstfruits of his father’s strength; the right of the firstborn belongs to him. (21:17).
If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who does not obey his father and mother and does not listen to them when disciplined, (21:18).
his father and mother are to lay hold of him and bring him to the elders of his city, to the gate of his hometown, (21:19).
and say to the elders, “This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious; he does not obey us. He is a glutton and a drunkard.” (21:20).
Then all the men of his city will stone him to death. So you must purge the evil from among you, and all Israel will hear and be afraid. (21:21).
If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is executed, and you hang his body on a tree, (21:22).

you must not leave the body on the tree overnight, but you must be sure to bury him that day, because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse. You must not defile the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance. (21:23).
crossRefs: Numbers 35:33: Bloodshed pollutes the land and nothing atones for it except the blood of the one who shed it, which is why an unsolved killing in 21:1-9 needs a rite at all.

Exodus 21:7-11: A woman brought into a household this way keeps her food, her clothing, and her marital rights, and goes out free without payment if they are withheld, the same refusal to let her be treated as property that 21:14 makes explicit.
Genesis 49:3-4: Reuben the firstborn forfeits his rank and Jacob says so to his face, the kind of case 21:15-17 legislates for.
Galatians 3:13: Paul quotes 21:23, 'Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree,' and applies it to the cross.
John 19:31: The bodies must not stay on the crosses over the Sabbath, so the legs are broken, and this law is being kept.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קִלְלַת אֱלֹהִים (qillat ʾElohim), Greek: κατάρα θεοῦ (katara theou), Aramaic: קללת אלהא (qillat alaha)
translationNotes.note: Being hanged exposed on a tree marked one as under God’s curse.

translationNotes.term: the heifer whose neck is broken
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה (eglah arufah)
translationNotes.note: For a murder with no known killer, the law gives the nearest town a public procedure (21:1-9). The elders measure to find which town is closest, take a heifer that has never worked, break its neck in a valley with running water that has never been plowed, and wash their hands over it while declaring they neither shed the blood nor saw it done. The washing of hands to disclaim responsibility for a death is the same gesture Pilate makes at Matthew 27:24.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תָּלָה עַל־עֵץ (talah al-ets)
translationNotes.note: This is not execution by hanging. The man is put to death first and the body is then hung up in public, which was the standard ancient way of turning a corpse into a warning: the Philistines fastened Saul's body to the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:10), and Joshua 8:29 and 10:26-27 do the same to defeated kings. Deuteronomy 21:23 requires the body down and buried the same day. Paul quotes that verse at Galatians 3:13, and John 19:31 records the bodies being taken down before sunset at the crucifixion.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֵאשִׁית אֹנוֹ (reshit ono), 'the beginning of his strength' - פִּי שְׁנַיִם (pi shenayim), a double portion
translationNotes.note: The words behind 'firstfruits' at 21:17 are not the harvest firstfruits (bikkurim) of Exodus 23:19 but a separate expression for a father's first son. Jacob speaks the same two words over Reuben at Genesis 49:3. Deuteronomy 21:15-17 bars a man with two wives from shifting the double portion off the actual firstborn onto the son of the wife he prefers, and it states the case with the firstborn belonging to the unloved wife. Genesis 49:3-4 shows Reuben losing the rank anyway, by his own act.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא־תִתְעַמֵּר בָּהּ (lo titammer bah), 'you shall not deal with her as merchandise'
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 21:10-14 puts a full month between capture and marriage: she shaves her head, trims her nails, puts off the clothing she was taken in, and mourns her father and mother. If the man then does not want her, he must let her go wherever she wishes, and 21:14 forbids two things by name, selling her for silver and treating her as goods. That second verb is rare; it stands again at Deuteronomy 24:7, describing what a kidnapper does to the man he has stolen. The word the law uses for the slaver's crime is the word it forbids here.

translationNotes.term: Brought to the elders at the gate
