His people have acted corruptly toward Him; the blemish on them is not that of His children, but of a perverse and crooked generation. (32:5).
Is this how you repay the LORD, O foolish and senseless people? Is He not your Father and Creator? Has He not made you and established you? (32:6).
Remember the days of old; consider the years long past. Ask your father, and he will tell you, your elders, and they will inform you. (32:7).
When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, when He divided the sons of man, He set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of God. (32:8).
But the LORD’s portion is His people, Jacob His allotted inheritance. (32:9).
He found him in a desert land, in a barren, howling wilderness; He surrounded him, He instructed him, He guarded him as the apple of His eye. (32:10).
As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young, He spread His wings to catch them and carried them on His pinions. (32:11).
The LORD alone led him, and no foreign god was with him. (32:12).
He made him ride on the heights of the land and fed him the produce of the field. He nourished him with honey from the rock and oil from the flinty crag, (32:13).

with curds from the herd and milk from the flock, with the fat of lambs, with rams from Bashan, and goats, with the choicest grains of wheat. From the juice of the finest grapes you drank the wine. (32:14).
But Jeshurun grew fat and kicked— becoming fat, bloated, and gorged. He abandoned the God who made him and scorned the Rock of his salvation. (32:15).
They provoked His jealousy with foreign gods; they enraged Him with abominations. (32:16).
They sacrificed to demons, not to God, to gods they had not known, to newly arrived gods, which your fathers did not fear. (32:17).
You ignored the Rock who brought you forth; you forgot the God who gave you birth. (32:18).
When the LORD saw this, He rejected them, provoked to anger by His sons and daughters. (32:19).
He said: “I will hide My face from them; I will see what will be their end. For they are a perverse generation— children of unfaithfulness. (32:20).

They have provoked My jealousy by that which is not God; they have enraged Me with their worthless idols. So I will make them jealous by those who are not a people; I will make them angry by a nation without understanding. (32:21).
For a fire has been kindled by My anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol; it consumes the earth and its produce, and scorches the foundations of the mountains. (32:22).
I will heap disasters upon them; I will spend My arrows against them. (32:23).
They will be wasted from hunger and ravaged by pestilence and bitter plague; I will send the fangs of wild beasts against them, with the venom of vipers that slither in the dust. (32:24).
Outside, the sword will take their children, and inside, terror will strike the young man and the young woman, the infant and the gray-haired man. (32:25).
I would have said that I would cut them to pieces and blot out their memory from mankind, (32:26).
if I had not dreaded the taunt of the enemy, lest their adversaries misunderstand and say: ‘Our own hand has prevailed; it was not the LORD who did all this.’” (32:27).
Israel is a nation devoid of counsel, with no understanding among them. (32:28).
If only they were wise, they would understand it; they would comprehend their fate. (32:29).
How could one man pursue a thousand, or two put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, unless the LORD had given them up? (32:30).
For their rock is not like our Rock, even our enemies concede. (32:31).
But their vine is from the vine of Sodom and from the fields of Gomorrah. Their grapes are poisonous; their clusters are bitter. (32:32).
Their wine is the venom of serpents, the deadly poison of cobras. (32:33).
“Have I not stored up these things, sealed up within My vaults? (32:34).
Vengeance is Mine; I will repay. In due time their foot will slip; for their day of disaster is near, and their doom is coming quickly.” (32:35).
For the LORD will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants when He sees that their strength is gone and no one remains, slave or free. (32:36).
He will say: “Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge, (32:37).
which ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their drink offerings? Let them rise up and help you; let them give you shelter! (32:38).
See now that I am He; there is no God besides Me. I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal, and there is no one who can deliver from My hand. (32:39).
For I lift up My hand to heaven and declare: As surely as I live forever, (32:40).
when I sharpen My flashing sword, and My hand grasps it in judgment, I will take vengeance on My adversaries and repay those who hate Me. (32:41).
I will make My arrows drunk with blood, while My sword devours flesh— the blood of the slain and captives, the heads of the enemy leaders.” (32:42).

Rejoice, O heavens, with Him, and let all God’s angels worship Him. Rejoice, O nations, with His people; for He will avenge the blood of His children. He will take vengeance on His adversaries and repay those who hate Him; He will cleanse His land and His people. (32:43).
Then Moses came with Joshua son of Nun and recited all the words of this song in the hearing of the people. (32:44).
When Moses had finished reciting all these words to all Israel, (32:45).
he said to them, “Take to heart all the words I have solemnly declared to you this day, so that you may command your children to carefully follow all the words of this law. (32:46).
For they are not idle words to you, because they are your life, and by them you will live long in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess.” (32:47).
On that same day the LORD said to Moses, (32:48).
“Go up into the Abarim Range to Mount Nebo, in the land of Moab across from Jericho, and view the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites as their own possession. (32:49).
And there on the mountain that you climb, you will die and be gathered to your people, just as your brother Aaron died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his people. (32:50).
For at the waters of Meribah-kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin, both of you broke faith with Me among the Israelites by failing to treat Me as holy in their presence. (32:51).
Although you shall see from a distance the land that I am giving the Israelites, you shall not enter it.” (32:52).
crossRefs: Numbers 20:9-13: The waters of Meribah, the reason given in 32:51 for barring Moses from the land.
Romans 10:19: Paul quotes 'I will make you jealous by those who are not a nation'.
Hebrews 10:30: Vengeance is Mine, I will repay, quoted from 32:35.
Revelation 15:3: They sing the song of Moses the servant of God and the song of the Lamb.
Psalm 78:1-8: A psalm that rehearses the same history so the next generation will not forget it.

translationNotes.term: I put to death and I make alive
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲנִי אָמִית וַאֲחַיֶּה (ʾanī ʾāmīt vaʾaḥayyeh), Greek (LXX): ἐγὼ ἀποκτενῶ καὶ ζῆν ποιήσω, Aramaic: אֲנָא מְמִית וּמְחַיֵּי
translationNotes.note: God claims sovereign power over life and death; this is not a human license to murder.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁירַת מֹשֶׁה (shirath Moshe), Greek: ᾆσμα Μωϋσῆ (asma Mōysē), Aramaic: שירת משה (shirath Moshe)
translationNotes.note: A prophetic song as witness against Israel’s unfaithfulness, declaring both God’s judgment and mercy.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּרַךְ (barakh), Greek: εὐλογέω (eulogeō), Aramaic: ברך (barakh)
translationNotes.note: To speak good or bestow benefit; Moses’ blessings call down God’s favor on each tribe.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּנִים אֶל־פָּנִים (panim el panim), Greek: πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον (prosōpon pros prosōpon), Aramaic: אנפין לקבל אנפין (anpin leqabel anpin)
translationNotes.note: Expression of direct, intimate encounter with God, unique to Moses among prophets.

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)

translationNotes.note: Ten thousand; also used idiomatically for 'countless.' Revelation 5:11's 'ten thousands of ten thousands' (myriades myriadon) of angels could be 100 million as a literal floor, though the intent is more naturally read as 'innumerable.'
translationNotes.original: Greek: μυριάς (myrias)

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses recites a song to Israel recounting God's faithful care, their ingratitude and idolatry, the curses that will follow, and God's eventual vindication; the LORD then tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo to view Canaan before his death, because Moses and Aaron broke faith at Meribah Kadesh.

stories.title: 🙏 Deuteronomy 33
summaryBullets: This is the blessing that Moses the man of God pronounced upon the Israelites before his death. (33:1).
He said: “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned upon us from Seir; He shone forth from Mount Paran and came with myriads of holy ones, with flaming fire at His right hand. (33:2).
Surely You love the people; all the holy ones are in Your hand, and they sit down at Your feet; each receives Your words — (33:3).
the law that Moses gave us, the possession of the assembly of Jacob. (33:4).
So the LORD became King in Jeshurun when the leaders of the people gathered, when the tribes of Israel came together. (33:5).
Let Reuben live and not die, nor his men be few.” (33:6).
And concerning Judah he said: “O LORD, hear the cry of Judah and bring him to his people. With his own hands he defends his cause, but may You be a help against his foes.” (33:7).
Concerning Levi he said: “Give Your Thummim to Levi and Your Urim to Your godly one, whom You tested at Massah and contested at the waters of Meribah. (33:8).
He said of his father and mother, ‘I do not consider them.’ He disregarded his brothers and did not know his own sons, for he kept Your word and maintained Your covenant. (33:9).
He will teach Your ordinances to Jacob and Your law to Israel; he will set incense before You and whole burnt offerings on Your altar. (33:10).
Bless his substance, O LORD, and accept the work of his hands. Smash the loins of those who rise against him, and of his foes so they can rise no more.” (33:11).
Concerning Benjamin he said: “May the beloved of the LORD rest secure in Him; God shields him all day long, and upon His shoulders he rests.” (33:12).
Concerning Joseph he said: “May his land be blessed by the LORD with the precious dew from heaven above and the deep waters that lie beneath, (33:13).
with the bountiful harvest from the sun and the abundant yield of the seasons, (33:14).
with the best of the ancient mountains and the bounty of the everlasting hills, (33:15).

with the choice gifts of the land and everything in it, and with the favor of Him who dwelt in the burning bush. May these rest on the head of Joseph and crown the brow of the prince of his brothers. (33:16).

His majesty is like a firstborn bull, and his horns are like those of a wild ox. With them he will gore the nations, even to the ends of the earth. Such are the myriads of Ephraim, and such are the thousands of Manasseh.” (33:17).
Concerning Zebulun he said: “Rejoice, Zebulun, in your journeys, and Issachar, in your tents. (33:18).
They will call the peoples to a mountain; there they will offer sacrifices of righteousness. For they will feast on the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand.” (33:19).
Concerning Gad he said: “Blessed is he who enlarges the domain of Gad! He lies down like a lion and tears off an arm or a head. (33:20).

He chose the best land for himself, because a ruler’s portion was reserved for him there. He came with the leaders of the people; he administered the LORD’s justice and His ordinances for Israel.” (33:21).
Concerning Dan he said: “Dan is a lion’s cub, leaping out of Bashan.” (33:22).
Concerning Naphtali he said: “Naphtali is abounding with favor, full of the blessing of the LORD; he shall take possession of the sea and the south.” (33:23).
And concerning Asher he said: “May Asher be the most blessed of sons; may he be the most favored among his brothers and dip his foot in oil. (33:24).
May the bolts of your gate be iron and bronze, and may your strength match your days.” (33:25).
“There is none like the God of Jeshurun, who rides the heavens to your aid, and the clouds in His majesty. (33:26).
The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms. He drives out the enemy before you, giving the command, ‘Destroy him!’ (33:27).
So Israel dwells securely; the fountain of Jacob lives untroubled in a land of grain and new wine, where even the heavens drip with dew. (33:28).

Blessed are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD? He is the shield that protects you, the sword in which you boast. Your enemies will cower before you, and you shall trample their high places.” (33:29).
crossRefs: Genesis 49:1-28: Jacob blesses the same twelve sons one by one before his death.
Exodus 28:30: The Urim and Thummim are placed in the breastpiece of judgment, the thing given to Levi in 33:8.
Judges 5:14-18: Deborah's song names the tribes and what each one did in the day of battle.
Numbers 6:22-27: The blessing Aaron and his sons are to speak over the people.
Joshua 13:1-33: The allotments east of the Jordan are assigned, beginning the division of the land.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְשֻׁרוּן (Yeshurun)
translationNotes.note: A poetic name for Israel built on the root yashar, straight or upright. It occurs only four times in the whole Old Testament, three of them in these chapters (Deuteronomy 32:15; 33:5; 33:26) and once in Isaiah 44:2. It is used here of a nation that has just been described in chapter 32 as anything but upright.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוּרִים וְתֻמִּים (Urim ve-Thummim)
translationNotes.note: Objects kept in the fold of the high priest's breastpiece and used to put a question to God and get an answer (Exodus 28:30; Leviticus 8:8). Saul uses them to identify the guilty party in 1 Samuel 14:41 and gets no answer from them at all in 1 Samuel 28:6. After the exile, families who could not prove priestly descent were barred from the holy food until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise (Ezra 2:63). The text never describes what they physically were.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַסָּה (Massah) - Hebrew: מְרִיבָה (Merivah)
translationNotes.note: Both are verdicts turned into place names. Massah means testing and Meribah means quarrelling, and Moses named the place at Rephidim with both words after Israel demanded water and asked whether the LORD was among them (Exodus 17:1-7). A second Meribah at Kadesh is where Moses struck the rock and was told he would not bring the assembly into the land (Numbers 20:1-13).

translationNotes.term: The horns of a wild ox
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְאֵם (reem)
translationNotes.note: The re'em is the aurochs, the wild ox of the ancient world: a bovine far larger than domestic cattle, with forward-curving horns, hunted by kings and impossible to yoke, which is the point Job 39:9-10 makes. The last one died in Poland in 1627. The Greek Septuagint rendered the word monokeros, one-horned, which is how the King James Version came to read unicorn.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁמֶן (shemen)
translationNotes.note: Asher's allotment was the coastal plain and hills of western Galilee, olive country. Oil was made by crushing the fruit under a rolling stone in a basin and then pressing the mash in baskets under a weighted beam, and it was food, lamp fuel, medicine, and soap in one. A man whose foot is in oil is standing in the press at the end of a good year.

stories.keyTakeaway: Before his death Moses blesses the tribes, Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun with Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher, recalling that the LORD came from Sinai with myriads of holy ones. He exalts the God of Jeshurun who rides the heavens to Israel’s help, the eternal God whose everlasting arms are underneath, and calls Israel blessed, a people saved by the LORD.

stories.title: 🙏 Deuteronomy 34
summaryBullets: Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which faces Jericho. And the LORD showed him the whole land — from Gilead as far as Dan, (34:1).
all of Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the Western Sea, (34:2).
the Negev, and the region from the Valley of Jericho (the City of Palms) all the way to Zoar. (34:3).

And the LORD said to him, “This is the land that I swore to give Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when I said, ‘I will give it to your descendants.’ I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross into it.” (34:4).
So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, as the LORD had said. (34:5).
And He buried him in a valley in the land of Moab facing Beth-peor, and no one to this day knows the location of his grave. (34:6).
Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died, yet his eyes were not weak, and his vitality had not diminished. (34:7).
The Israelites grieved for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, until the time of weeping and mourning for Moses came to an end. (34:8).
Now Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. So the Israelites obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses. (34:9).
Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face— (34:10).
no prophet who did all the signs and wonders that the LORD sent Moses to do in the land of Egypt to Pharaoh and to all his officials and all his land, (34:11).
and no prophet who performed all the mighty acts of power and awesome deeds that Moses did in the sight of all Israel. (34:12).
crossRefs: Numbers 27:12-14: Moses is told to go up the mountain, see the land, and then be gathered to his people.
Deuteronomy 3:23-28: Moses pleads to be allowed to cross, and is told to look from Pisgah instead.
Joshua 1:1-2: After the death of Moses the LORD tells Joshua to get up and cross this Jordan.
Jude 1:9: Michael the archangel disputes with the devil over the body of Moses.
Matthew 17:1-3: Moses appears with Elijah on the mountain, talking with Jesus.

translationNotes.term: Mount Nebo, the top of Pisgah
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְבוֹ (Nevo) - Hebrew: פִּסְגָּה (Pisgah)
translationNotes.note: Nebo is a headland on the western edge of the Moabite plateau, east of the north end of the Dead Sea, standing about 2,300 feet above sea level and some 3,700 feet above the Jordan valley floor immediately below it. Pisgah is the ridge it belongs to. From the summit the Jordan valley, Jericho, and the hills of Judah are visible on a clear day, which is what verses 1 to 3 are describing.

translationNotes.term: The Valley of Jericho, the City of Palms
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִיר הַתְּמָרִים (Ir ha-Temarim)
translationNotes.note: Jericho sits in the Jordan rift about 850 feet below sea level, the lowest town on earth, watered year-round by a strong spring in an otherwise arid basin. Its date palms and balsam made it valuable enough to be fought over for centuries, and the name City of Palms is used for it again in Judges 1:16 and 3:13.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית פְּעוֹר (Beit Peor)
translationNotes.note: Peor is the height in Moab where Balak took Balaam to look down on Israel and curse them (Numbers 23:28), and Baal-peor is the local god whose worship Israel joined at the end of that episode. Numbers 25:1-9 records the result: sacrificial meals with the women of Moab, bowing to their gods, and twenty-four thousand dead in the plague that followed. Moses is buried within sight of the place.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵבֶל (evel)
translationNotes.note: Mourning was a fixed public observance with a set length, not a private mood: torn clothes, sackcloth, dust or ashes, fasting, and wailing. Seven days was the ordinary term (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13). Thirty days was reserved for the greatest figures, and Aaron received the same thirty (Numbers 20:29). Jacob was embalmed in Egypt and mourned seventy days there (Genesis 50:3).

translationNotes.term: Because Moses had laid his hands on him
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סָמַךְ (samakh)
translationNotes.note: Samakh means to lean or press down with weight, not to touch lightly. Numbers 27:18-23 records the ceremony: Joshua set before Eleazar the priest and the whole assembly, hands laid on him, and some of Moses' authority given to him publicly so that Israel would obey. The same verb is used of the worshipper pressing his hand on the head of his offering (Leviticus 1:4).

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses views the promised land from Mount Nebo, is told he will not enter it, and dies in Moab at age 120; Joshua succeeds him as the Israelites mourn for thirty days.

intro:
Deuteronomy (Hebrew: Devarim, "Words") was written by Moses on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River and opposite Jericho, in the final weeks of his life around 1406 BC. Moses was 120 years old, and the original Exodus generation had died in the wilderness over the preceding forty years. Israel stood on the eastern shore of the Jordan, ready to cross into Canaan under Joshua's leadership. Moses delivered a series of public addresses to the new generation beginning on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year after the Exodus (around January-February 1405 BC), and recorded them as he spoke. The historical setting is the eastern frontier of Canaan in the Late Bronze Age, with the Israelites encamped near Mount Nebo, the Canaanite city-states across the Jordan to the west, the kingdom of Moab to the south, and the kingdom of Ammon to the east. Jewish tradition holds that the closing verses recording Moses' death were added by his successor Joshua. Jesus and the apostles attribute the Pentateuch, including Deuteronomy, to Moses (Mark 12:26, Luke 24:44, John 5:46, Romans 10:5).

Deuteronomy is the fifth and final book of the Pentateuch (the five books of Moses). Its Hebrew name Devarim comes from the opening words of the book, following the ancient Jewish convention of titling books by their opening line; the English title "Deuteronomy" comes from the Greek Septuagint translation Deuteronomion (3rd century BC), meaning "second law" or "repetition of the law." Hebrew manuscript fragments of Deuteronomy were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 2nd and 1st centuries BC.
